title: Pre-Transfer CTA and Futile Transfers in the Drip-and-Ship Model: Triage Precision, Workflow Trade-offs, and a Persistent Gray Zone
abstract: Background Patients not receiving endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) after interhospital transfer in a "drip-and-ship" stroke network place a burden on the system. The impact of pre-transfer computed tomography angiography (CTA) at the primary stroke center (PSC) on transfer outcomes and workflow efficiency has not been well characterized. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 314 acute ischemic stroke patients transferred for potential EVT within the Tainan-Chiayi Stroke Network (October 2021-September 2025). Patients were stratified by CTA timing: pre-transfer (n=66) versus post-transfer (n=248). Workflow time metrics were compared. Transfers not followed by EVT were classified into three categories: potentially avoidable, physiologically unavoidable, and gray zone. Results Among transferred patients, pre-transfer CTA was associated with a higher EVT treatment yield (72.7% vs. 33.9%; P<0.001), but a longer PSC door-in-door-out time (140 vs. 88 min; P<0.001). In multivariable analysis, post-transfer CTA remained the strongest independent predictor of not undergoing EVT (aOR 5.21; 95% CI 2.83-9.60). Among transfers not followed by EVT in the post-transfer CTA group, 40.2% were classified as potentially avoidable due to the absence of an actionable occlusion. Gray zone scenarios, driven primarily by large infarct cores, intracranial atherosclerotic disease and medium vessel occlusion, constituted the dominant remaining category in both groups. Conclusion Pre-transfer CTA was associated with a higher EVT treatment yield but a longer PSC processing time. The persistent gray zone requires strategies beyond imaging alone, and the trade-off between triage precision and transfer efficiency warrants ongoing evaluation across diverse stroke network settings.

title: Effects of calf neuromuscular electrostimulation on hemodynamics and systemic fibrinolytic activity: a randomized clinical pilot study
abstract: Muscular physical exercise is a stimulus to circulatory development. But it is not always possible. In this context, there was the development of intermittent pneumatic compression therapy and, more recently, neuromuscular electrical stimulation. A clinical, interventional, prospective, single-center, randomized, single-blind study was carried out to evaluate the effect of neuromuscular electrical stimulation on lower limb hemodynamics and systemic fibrinolytic activity in 10 healthy subjects. The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Botucatu Medical School, UNESP (CAAE: 30680120.0.0000.5411). The flow volume variation was significant, in the joint analysis of the limbs, at the popliteal vein. The diameter of the vessels proved to be the most sensitive to neuromuscular electrical stimulation in the joint analysis of the limbs. Flow velocities varied statistically significantly only in the femoral vessels. In the popliteal vessels, there was a variation in flow increment, but it was not statistically significant. There was no statistically significant change in the plasminogen activator inhibitor. For plasminogen activator, there was numerical variation, with continuous increment, but this did not represent a statistically significant change (p > 0.05). There was no adverse event and all subjects had the lowest tolerance score (no feeling of discomfort). NMES significantly improved popliteal and femoral hemodynamics. Although numerical increases in plasminogen activator were observed, they did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). The protocol proved to be safe and well-tolerated. Trial registration: Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC) RBR-6gs4bdh. UTN U1111-1301-5055. Registered on January 29, 2024. URL: https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/RBR-6gs4bdh.

title: First-line discontinuation and subsequent therapy in the era of upfront intensification for metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: a real-world analysis
abstract: Aim: Treatment intensification has become standard first-line therapy for metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC). However, real-world discontinuation patterns and their impact on subsequent treatment remain insufficiently characterized. We aimed to evaluate first-line discontinuation and subsequent therapy administration rates in clinical practice. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study analyzed 1,067 patients in the AGEHA real-world database. Patients received either androgen deprivation therapy ± bicalutamide (ADT/CAB) or upfront intensification therapy including androgen receptor pathway inhibitors or docetaxel. The primary endpoint was the first-line discontinuation rate. First-line discontinuation was defined as permanent discontinuation because of progressive disease (PD), adverse events (AEs), death, or other documented reasons. The secondary endpoint was the subsequent therapy administration rate among patients who discontinued first-line treatment. Results: Among 1,056 eligible patients, 643 received upfront intensification therapy and 413 received ADT/CAB as a historical reference cohort. In the upfront intensification cohort, first-line discontinuation occurred in 338 patients (52.6%) and varied markedly across regimens, ranging from 28.1% with ADT plus enzalutamide to 84.7% with ADT plus docetaxel. Subsequent therapy administration after discontinuation also differed across upfront intensification regimens, ranging from 44.1% with ADT plus enzalutamide to 77.3% with ADT plus apalutamide. Heterogeneous transition patterns, including AE-related discontinuation, switching without PD, best supportive care (BSC) after PD, and death, were observed. In the historical ADT/CAB reference cohort, first-line discontinuation and subsequent therapy administration rates were 62.2% and 63.0%, respectively. Conclusions: In the upfront intensification era, first-line discontinuation and subsequent treatment transitions showed substantial heterogeneity across regimens. AE-related discontinuation and switching without PD created treatment pathways that are not fully captured by conventional second-line therapy analyses. The ADT/CAB cohort served as a historical reference rather than a contemporary comparator, and differences between cohorts should therefore be interpreted with caution.

title: Locoregional administration of bispecific CAR-T cells targeting CD44 and CD133 in recurrent high-grade glioma: a first-in-human investigator-initiated trial
abstract: Grade IV glioma remains highly lethal, and effective therapies for recurrent disease remain limited. Glioma stem cells (GSCs) contribute to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence, providing a rationale for GSC-targeted immunotherapy. We conducted a single-center, single-arm investigator-initiated trial evaluating locoregional administration of CD44/CD133 bispecific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells incorporating a truncated interleukin-7 receptor α (IL-7Rα) intracellular domain in ten adults with recurrent grade IV glioma. Treatment was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities or Grade ≥2 cytokine release syndrome. Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, and no patient required IL-6 or IL-1 blockade. CAR-T cell leakage into peripheral blood remained minimal, whereas cerebrospinal fluid cytokine elevations were modest following infusion. Three patients achieved partial responses. The median overall survival after the first CAR-T cell infusion was 465 days. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses suggested patient stratification in macrophage-associated signatures, particularly in interferon signaling and antigen-presentation programs, which were associated with distinct clinical outcomes independently of IDH mutation status in this cohort. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and safety of repeated locoregional administration of GSC-targeting IL-7Rα-armored bispecific CAR-T cells. Exploratory immune profiling further identified inter-patient heterogeneity in macrophage-associated immune programs, which warrants validation in larger prospective studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05577091, NMPA No. CXSL2500032).

title: Pathological response and survival outcomes of three neoadjuvant strategies for resectable EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: Background The optimal neoadjuvant strategy for resectable epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains uncertain. We compared pathological response and survival outcomes across three neoadjuvant strategies. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 186 patients with resectable stage II–IIIB EGFR-mutant NSCLC who initiated neoadjuvant therapy between 2020 and 2024. The regimens were neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NCT), neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT), or neoadjuvant EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor plus chemotherapy (NTT). Of these patients, 166 underwent definitive resection. Major pathological response (MPR) served as the primary endpoint, whereas secondary outcomes comprised pathological complete response (pCR), recurrence-free survival (RFS), overall survival (OS), and safety. Analyses used propensity score matching (PSM), Kaplan–Meier estimation, and Cox regression. Results The resection rates were 83.0%, 90.9%, and 93.3% for NCT, NICT, and NTT, respectively (P = 0.234). Among resected patients, the MPR rates were 6.8%, 27.5%, and 23.8%, and the pCR rates were 0%, 18.8%, and 14.3%, respectively. At a median follow-up of 35 months, the 3-year RFS estimates were 50.7%, 59.6%, and 87.8%, and the 3-year OS estimates were 71.1%, 90.0%, and 94.2%, respectively. After PSM, OS and RFS curves differed between NTT and NCT (log-rank P = 0.0359 and P = 0.0193) and between NTT and NICT (P = 0.0487 and P = 0.0464). In the primary multivariable model, NTT was associated with lower OS event risk (HR = 0.262, P = 0.040) and RFS event risk (HR = 0.339, P = 0.010) versus NCT. In a sensitivity model, the RFS association persisted (HR = 0.354, P = 0.016), whereas the OS association was attenuated (HR = 0.312, P = 0.082). Any-cause adverse events (AEs) occurred in 38/53, 64/88, and 30/45 patients; grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs occurred in 1, 3, and 0 patients, respectively. Conclusion Among resected patients, NICT and NTT were associated with higher pathological response rates than NCT. An association between NTT and lower recurrence risk was observed, but residual confounding, limited events, and unadjusted postoperative therapy preclude causal conclusions or claims of treatment superiority.

title: Enhancing Nursing Education Through Multi-Specialty Faculty Clinical Placements in Oncology, Emergency and Critical Care Nursing
abstract: Background: Internationalization of nursing education provides opportunities for faculty development, knowledge exchange, and exposure to alternative approaches to academic and clinical practice. However, evidence documenting lecturers’ experiences and the potential educational value of international faculty exchange, particularly in resource-constrained settings, remains limited. This study describes lecturers’ experiences during a multi-specialty international academic and clinical exchange. Methods: The experiences of three faculty members from the University of Zambia, School of Nursing Sciences, who participated in an international capacity-strengthening exchange programme under the Strengthening Health Professional Workforce Education Programs for Improved Health Care in Zambia initiative where documented. The exchange was conducted in collaboration with Birmingham City University (BCU), United Kingdom, from 12 August to 8 September 2024. Participants were faculty involved in postgraduate nursing education in oncology and palliative care, trauma and emergency nursing, and critical care nursing. Data were derived from participants’ written accounts, structured placement schedules, and an exchange mission report documenting academic activities, simulation-based learning, professional engagements, and observational clinical placements across BCU and National Health Service institutions in Birmingham and surrounding areas. Results: The exchange provided exposure to postgraduate nursing curricula, simulation and skills laboratory education, multidisciplinary practice, patient pathways, clinical protocols, mentorship, advanced nursing roles, and specialist clinical services. In oncology and palliative care, participants observed chemotherapy, radiotherapy, acute oncology, apheresis, stem-cell services, Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter line care, hospice care, and oncology research. Emergency and critical care experiences included patient navigation, triage, resuscitation, sepsis management, advanced monitoring, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, standardized protocols, checklists, multidisciplinary reviews, and critical care outreach. Participants identified several practices with potential for contextual adaptation, including structured mentorship, simulation-based education, clinical protocols, patient navigation, quality improvement, and strengthened clinical reasoning. Conclusion: International faculty exchange provided valuable opportunities for professional learning, reflection, networking, and identification of contextually relevant approaches to strengthening nursing education. Sustained institutional support, structured knowledge translation, and evaluation of post-exchange implementation are recommended.

title: Spontaneous pneumomediastinum following childhood-onset vaping: a case of developmental pulmonary vulnerability
abstract: A 15-year-old male presented to the emergency department with acute chest and epigastric pain following severe vomiting. His history included daily e-cigarette use beginning at age 8, during the critical alveolarization window of lung development. CT imaging showed extensive pneumomediastinum, bilateral apical pneumothoraces, severe subcutaneous emphysema, and pneumorrhachis, a particularly severe set of barotrauma findings. Conservative management with high-flow oxygen, intravenous antibiotics, and supportive care achieved complete clinical resolution within 5 days. This case raises the hypothesis that childhood-onset vaping during pulmonary maturation may be a risk factor for severe barotrauma, although product composition, concurrent substance use and individual susceptibility may also contribute. The developmental vulnerability hypothesis may change how clinicians should assess risk and counsel young vapers, particularly those with pre-adolescent onset of use.

title: Long-Term Multimodality Imaging Reveals Heterogeneous Myocardial Responses During Disease-Specific Therapy for Fabry Disease: A Case Report
abstract: Background Cardiac involvement in Fabry disease is heterogeneous and characterised by left ventricular hypertrophy, microvascular dysfunction, and progressive myocardial remodelling. Although disease-specific therapies may modify the underlying disease process, their long-term effects on different myocardial components remain underexplored. Case summary A man in his 50s presented with chest discomfort. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular hypertrophy, and diastolic dysfunction, suggesting infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Markedly reduced α-galactosidase A activity confirmed Fabry disease. Enzyme replacement therapy resolved symptoms, and resting coronary Doppler findings were consistent with favourable changes in coronary flow dynamics. After 3 years, treatment was transitioned to pharmacological chaperone therapy, which was continued for 6 years. During long-term follow-up, left ventricular global longitudinal strain declined before a reduction in LVEF. Serial cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a reduction in low-T1 areas and a relative expansion of high-T1 areas. The distribution of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) remained unchanged. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I and plasma lyso-Gb3 levels remained stable throughout follow-up. Despite subclinical deterioration in cardiac and renal function, the patient remained clinically stable without major adverse events. Discussion This case highlights heterogeneous myocardial responses during long-term disease-specific therapy for Fabry disease. Serial multimodality imaging demonstrated dynamic changes in native T1 abnormalities, whereas the distribution of LGE remained stable. Despite sustained clinical stability, persistent low-grade myocardial injury and progressive impairment of left ventricular deformation were observed during follow-up. Different myocardial components may follow distinct longitudinal trajectories during therapy. Multimodality imaging is important for comprehensive assessment of Fabry cardiomyopathy.

title: Digital health tools in epidemiology and public health in Poland: Effectiveness, availability, and implementation barriers – a narrative review
abstract: Introduction and aim. The synthesis of current scientific evidence on the effectiveness, implementation and barriers associated with digital health interventions, with particular focus on health outcomes, system efficiency, user engagement and digital inequalities, with emphasis on the Polish public health and epidemiological context. Methods of review. A structured narrative literature review was conducted based on peer-reviewed scientific articles from the PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Embase databases (publications from 2021-2026), including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies and policy analyses. Data were subjected to narrative synthesis within thematic areas. Brief summary of current knowledge. Out of the 1,247 identified records, 34 publications were included in the analysis. Digital health interventions show moderate to high effectiveness in improving selected clinical outcomes, screening rates, and patient engagement. Patient portals and mHealth tools are associated with improved self-management and system efficiency. Persistent barriers include limited interoperability, regulatory fragmentation, data privacy concerns and digital inequalities disproportionately affecting older adults and populations with low digital literacy. Summary. Digital health technologies offer measurable benefits, but their full utilisation requires a systemic resolution of interoperability, standardisation and digital literacy problems. Evidence-based implementation is needed to support their effective and equitable use.

title: General practitioner attitudes towards the utility of artificial intelligence-augmented clinical decision support for hypertension in Australia and England: a qualitative study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a persistent global health concern; in Australia, over half of hypertensive patients experience poor blood pressure control (≥140/90 mmHg). Given that hypertension is predominantly managed in primary care, it may represent an ideal setting for implementing novel artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented clinical decision support tools (CDST) for hypertension management. We aimed to explore GP attitudes and experiences on the acceptability and usability of AI-augmented CDST for medication advice in hypertension management. METHODS: This qualitative exploratory study in two jurisdictions with similar primary care settings (Australia and England) used purposive sampling to promote diversity of views. Semi-structured interviews, including two scenarios of AI-augmented CDST, were analysed with thematic analysis. RESULTS: A total of 22 GPs (Australia 14, England 8) were recruited through existing professional networks. GP attitudes towards AI in primary care hypertension management reflected their pragmatic, patient-centred approach within their specific sociocultural context. Clear country differences reflected a more 'protocolised' approach in England, and a more sceptical perception of the quality and applicability of primary care data Australia. GPs in both countries considered an AI tool broadly trustworthy if endorsed by trusted clinical associations, and highlighted that tools would have limited utility if they could not offer efficiencies (e.g. seamless interoperability and synthesis of patient data in relation to clinical recommendations) that supported the management of complexity for their specific patients. CONCLUSION: For AI-augmented CDST to be adopted in primary care, it must align with the workflow, time constraints and relational nature of general practice, while supporting context-sensitive, individualised decision-making.

title: Procalcitonin-Guided Antibiotic Initiation in Adults Presenting to Emergency Departments With Suspected Infection: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
abstract: Emergency physicians must balance timely treatment of bacterial infection against unnecessary antibiotic prescribing. We systematically reviewed randomized controlled trials evaluating whether procalcitonin-guided care changes initial antibiotic initiation or prescription in adults presenting to emergency departments with suspected infection. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP were searched from inception through August 25, 2026. Trials were pooled when outcome definitions were sufficiently comparable, using random-effects meta-analysis with modified Hartung–Knapp confidence intervals. Ten trials (13,286 participants) were included; four respiratory infection trials (3,602 participants) contributed to the primary synthesis. Procalcitonin-guided care reduced initial antibiotic initiation or prescription (risk ratio, 0.87; 95% confidence interval, 0.82–0.92; I²=0%; high-certainty evidence), corresponding to approximately 89 fewer patients receiving or being prescribed antibiotics per 1,000. Sensitivity analyses produced similar estimates. For 28- to 30-day mortality, the pooled risk ratio across five trials was 0.92 (95% confidence interval, 0.57–1.49; low-certainty evidence); estimates for intensive care unit admission and antibiotic-related adverse events were imprecise. This updated review provides a decision-specific estimate of reduced initial antibiotic prescribing in emergency department respiratory infections and clarifies how differences in outcome definitions, trial designs, and patient populations affect interpretation of earlier syntheses. Effects on mortality and other clinical outcomes remain uncertain overall, and the respiratory prescribing estimate should not be extrapolated to undifferentiated fever, suspected sepsis, or acute heart failure.

title: Development and external validation of an interpretable machine learning score for early sepsis identification in the emergency department: a multicentre retrospective cohort study
abstract: Importance Sepsis is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Timely recognition and treatment in the emergency department (ED), often referred to as the “golden window,” are critical to improving outcomes. Yet, current diagnostic tools either demonstrate limited accuracy or rely on laboratory results that are not immediately available during initial ED evaluation, constraining rapid and reliable sepsis identification in the ED. Objective To develop and externally validate a data-driven interpretable score for early identification of sepsis in the ED across three large health systems. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from three health systems. The primary derivation cohort included all ED visits at 11 hospitals within the M Health Fairview system (Minnesota, 2019-2025). Two external cohorts include ED visits from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC, Boston, 2011-2019) extracted from the MIMIC-IV-ED database, and ED visits from the Stanford Health Care (Stanford, 2020-2022) sourced from the MC-MED database. In our analysis, completed in August 2025, we developed the Emergency Sepsis Risk Prediction (ESRP) score using the AutoScore framework. We evaluated its performance against commonly used bedside tools, including quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA), National Early Warning Score (NEWS), the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS), and the Rapid Emergency Medicine Score (REMS), as well as logistic regression (LR) and random forest (RF) models. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was sepsis diagnosis during the ED or hospital stay, determined from ICD-9 and ICD-10 discharge codes. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Results The study included a total of 2,193,244 ED visits across three sites: 1,626,055 in the Minnesota cohort (1,271,865 for model derivation, and 354,190 for internal validation), and 448,804 and 118,385 in the BIDMC and Stanford external validation cohorts, respectively. In Minnesota internal validation, the ESRP score achieved an AUROC of 0.820 (95% CI, 0.810– 0.825) and an AUPRC of 0.054 (95% CI, 0.051–0.058). In the BIDMC cohort, the ESRP achieved an AUROC of 0.838 (95% CI, 0.833–0.842), compared with 0.636 (95% CI, 0.633– 0.640) for qSOFA and 0.760 (95% CI, 0.757–0.765) for NEWS. In the Stanford cohort, the ESRP achieved an AUROC of 0.892 (95% CI, 0.887–0.898), compared with 0.697 (95% CI, 0.684–0.716) for qSOFA and 0.870 (95% CI, 0.861–0.881) for NEWS. Conclusions The ESRP score, based on 10 easily obtainable triage variables, provided accurate, generalizable, and interpretable early sepsis identification across diverse ED populations. Its simplicity and strong performance suggest potential for integration into routine ED triage workflows to support timely sepsis care.

title: Postictal hemispheric hypoperfusion mimicking a large ischemic core on computed tomography perfusion: a case report
abstract: Background Incomplete computed tomography perfusion (CTP) acquisition can cause truncation artifacts. We report a case of stroke mimicry with postictal hypoperfusion exhibiting paradoxical pseudo-normalization on CTP due to vulnerabilities in postprocessing algorithms. Case Report An 85-year-old woman presented with left hemiplegia (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score, 17). Premature CTP termination truncated the delayed time-attenuation curve (TAC) in the right hemisphere. In RAPID algorithms calculating the mean transit time (MTT) as cerebral blood volume (CBV)/cerebral blood flow, truncation causes a disproportionate CBV underestimation and falsely shortens the right MTT. This creates a paradoxical pattern in which the normal left hemisphere appears falsely delayed. Conversely, JLK-CTP yielded perfusion maps that more closely reflected the expected right-sided hypoperfusion in this case. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed right-sided infarcts, and electroencephalography revealed ipsilateral epileptiform discharges. After antiepileptic treatment, her NIHSS score improved to 4. Conclusion Short CTP acquisition during marked perfusion delay induces truncation artifacts and pseudo-normalization. Clinicians must review raw TACs and understand the differences between postprocessing algorithms to avoid misinterpretation.

title: Stellate ganglion block may reduce postoperative pain and attenuate early declines in cognitive function after laparoscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether stellate ganglion block (SGB) improves postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery. Methods Embase, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed were searched through 13 July 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing perioperative SGB with sham block or no block in laparoscopic surgical patients. Risk of bias was evaluated with RoB 2. Postoperative pain, cognitive function, postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), and gastrointestinal recovery were synthesized using mean differences (MDs), standardized mean differences (SMDs), or relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Analyses were performed in R version 4.6.1. Results Forty-three RCTs involving 3,733 participants were included. SGB reduced resting pain at 24 h (SMD = −0.67, 95% CI [−1.16, −0.18]) and rescue analgesic use (RR = 0.63, 95% CI [0.41, 0.97]). It was also associated with smaller postoperative declines in MMSE scores (calculated as preoperative minus postoperative scores) at 24 h (MD = −2.16 points, 95% CI [−2.97, −1.36]) and 72 h (MD = −2.86 points, 95% CI [−4.03, −1.68]), and with shorter time to first flatus (MD = −9.03 h, 95% CI [−12.50, −5.56]) and bowel-sound recovery (MD = −9.27 h, 95% CI [−13.33, −5.21]). Subgroup analysis suggested differences in time to first flatus by surgical type (P < 0.0001). SGB also reduced PONV and rescue antiemetic use. Conclusion Perioperative SGB may be associated with improvements in postoperative pain, early cognitive function, gastrointestinal recovery, and PONV after laparoscopic surgery. However, the certainty of evidence was low or very low for most outcomes, and all included RCTs were conducted in China. Given the substantial heterogeneity and limited generalizability, current evidence does not yet support the routine perioperative use of SGB. Further high-quality, multicenter RCTs involving diverse populations are warranted. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261441978, identifier CRD420261441978

title: Case Report: CD19-directed immunotherapy sequencing in multiply relapsed pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia: treatment burden, access, and continuity of care in Brazil
abstract: Background CD19-directed immunotherapies have transformed the treatment of pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). However, in countries where access is heterogeneous, the interval between evidence, indication and actual delivery may expose children to avoidable treatment burden before immunotherapy is finally used. Case presentation We report the therapeutic course of a male patient diagnosed with B-ALL at 10 years of age in Brazil. After initial treatment, he developed a first medullary relapse after 35 months and later a second relapse during relapse-therapy maintenance. He was refractory to intensive chemotherapy but achieved measurable residual disease (MRD) negativity after two cycles of blinatumomab, allowing haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). The post-HSCT course was marked by grade IV acute graft-versus-host disease, prolonged intensive care, invasive ventilation, severe BK-virus hemorrhagic cystitis requiring urologic procedures, viral reactivations, invasive fungal and bacterial infections, intestinal pneumatosis and severe malnutrition. One year later, he developed combined bone marrow and central nervous system (CNS) relapse. After low-intensity bridging therapy, bone marrow disease was reduced to MRD 0.0032% and CNS remission was achieved before CD19 CAR T-cell infusion. Grade 2 cytokine release syndrome occurred with fever and fluid-responsive hypotension, without documented neurotoxicity; he was discharged on day +10 and remained in bone marrow and CNS remission nine months after infusion. He died approximately nine months after infusion, from pulmonary complications of COVID-19 while leukemia remained in bone marrow and CNS remission. Conclusion This case illustrates that the clinical value of immunotherapy is inseparable from timing. Recent frontline blinatumomab data reinforce that, for selected children, precision immunotherapy should not be viewed only as salvage after cumulative chemotherapy toxicity. The right treatment, delivered at the right time, may reduce both clinical and economic burden while preserving therapeutic opportunity.

title: Warm or cold blood cardioplegia: does temperature really matter?
abstract: Background The optimal temperature for blood cardioplegia in cardiac surgery remains controversial. Although both warm- and cold-blood cardioplegia are widely used, convincing evidence demonstrating the superiority of either strategy is lacking. Objective To critically review the experimental, metabolic, and clinical evidence comparing warm- and cold-blood cardioplegia and to assess whether temperature influences clinical outcomes. Methods We reviewed experimental studies, mechanistic investigations, randomised controlled trials, and meta-analyses evaluating myocardial protection with warm- and cold-blood cardioplegia, focusing on myocardial metabolism, biochemical markers of injury, postoperative cardiac function, and clinical outcomes. Studies were appraised using a structured framework that distinguishes evidence on temperature itself from evidence on combined cardioplegia strategies. Conclusions Randomised trials and meta-analyses have not detected significant differences in mortality, perioperative myocardial infarction or major adverse cardiac events, although none was designed to establish equivalence. Warm blood cardioplegia is associated with improved myocardial metabolism, lower surrogate biochemical markers of injury, and enhanced early postoperative cardiac function, whereas cold blood cardioplegia provides superior metabolic suppression and acid–base stability during prolonged ischaemia. These surrogate differences have not translated into improved clinical outcomes. Because temperature is frequently varied together with vehicle, route and dosing, its independent contribution often remains uncertain. Rather than a universal preference for one technique, the choice of cardioplegic temperature should be guided by patient characteristics, operative complexity, anticipated ischaemic duration, and institutiona experience.

title: Commentary: Drug shortage: causes, impact, and mitigation strategies
abstract: Shukar et al. (2021) synthesize a decade of global evidence on drug shortages into a supply-, demand-, and regulatory-side causal framework, and document mitigation strategies ranging from institutional stock management to national advance-notification systems. Their most consequential finding, however, is methodological: research on drug shortages is concentrated in high-income countries. Low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) are represented by only a handful of studies, and low-income countries are almost entirely absent from the evidence base.Libya illustrates this gap acutely. No Libyan study appears in the review's synthesis, and no official national shortage-surveillance system exists in the country. Yet fragmented facility-level and institutional data -Ministry of Health reports, WHO collaborations, and independent surveys (Morato Bermejo andBarbi, 2024, WHO, 2019) indicate a shortage crisis at least as severe as the review's higher-income case studies, and it maps closely onto their causal framework. This Commentary uses Libya to test that framework in a data-poor, conflict-affected setting, and argues that closing this evidence gap is a precondition for translating the review's mitigation strategies into practice.Libya's constraints are not unique. Comparable conflict-affected LMICs show similar patterns of import dependence and collapsed supply infrastructure: a facility survey in Yemen found essential medicines available only 52.8% of the time amid ongoing conflict (Mohamed Ibrahim et al., 2020), and Sudan's pharmaceutical sector has been described as facing a humanitarian catastrophe since the 2023 civil war, with local manufacturing halted and no functioning reporting system (Hemmeda et al., 2024). Libya's case therefore speaks to conditions well beyond its own borders.Supply-side. Libya has no domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing base, public or private; it is entirely import-dependent, a more extreme version of the "unavailability of raw material" and "manufacturing issues" categories the review documents in Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. The review's observation that low-profitability medicines (generics, injectables) are systematically under-supplied is consistent with reports of shortages in commercially unattractive medicines in Libya, including orphan drugs (Ismail et al., 2025) .Demand-side and regulatory. The review's warning that single-supplier tendering and group procurement can disrupt purchasing patterns corresponds closely to Libya's centralized procurement structure, in which facility-level requests flow through the Ministry of Health's Pharmacy Directorate to the Medical Supply Authority, which manages tendering and distributes medicines through five regional branches (El Oakley et al., 2013, HIDC, 2023). Facility-level needs assessments are reportedly submitted irregularly rather than on the intended annual cycle (Allen et al., 2024, Elkalmi, 2025). Since mid-2026, Libya's Ministry of Health has engaged in consultations with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention toward joining the African Pooled Purchasing Mechanism (APPM) (Zaptia, 2026); should Libya proceed, the review's warning about group-procurement disruption is directly relevant to how the mechanism is evaluated. This would not be Libya's first such experience: a five-country consortium (Morocco, Mauritania, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya) formed in 1981 issued its first tender in 1982 but failed to develop effectively because of logistical constraints (Khoja and Bawazir, 2005) -a precedent the APPM discussions should not repeat.Regulatory fragmentation compounds these pressures: the absence of a robust national drug policy has been linked to weak market oversight, counterfeit-medicine circulation, and poorly regulated marketing (El Oakley et al., 2013, Elfituri et al., 2018, Kafu, 2014), echoing the review's point that weak regulatory frameworks are themselves a driver of shortage risk.Absent the kind of national reporting infrastructure the review documents in the United States and parts of Europe, Libya's evidence base consists of isolated facility-level assessments. A 2018 survey of Libyan pharmacists found that 90% of respondents believed key pharmaceutical products were not accessible in the public sector, 60% considered private-market medicines unaffordable, and 80% distrusted government quality-control procedures; most also reported irrational prescribing, dispensing, and use (Elfituri et al., 2018). A more recent Tripoli survey found originator cardiovascular medicines available in only 25.6% of pharmacies and generics in 55.9%, with prices up to 7.4 times international reference values (Dyab et al., 2026). These figures are broadly consistent with, and in places more severe than, the availability gaps the review documents elsewhere in LMICs. What distinguishes Libya is less the shortage's severity than the near-total absence of the systematic reporting infrastructure the review treats as foundational to its mitigation strategies.Shukar et al. ( 2021) call for international cooperation on a mitigation plan that includes LMICspecific strategies, and for LMICs to develop advance-notification, reporting, and tracking systems. Libya's case qualifies this recommendation: in a conflict-affected state with no domestic manufacturing capacity and a damaged institutional base, the starting point cannot be the reporting infrastructure higher-capacity countries have built incrementally. Armed conflict since 2011 has directly damaged health facilities and disrupted pharmaceutical services (Daw et al., 2016, El-Mogassabi andKaziri, 2025), while broader institutional challenges continue to affect hospital management and administrative accountability (Salem and Sulayman, 2025); shortage mitigation here depends first on rebuilding basic institutional and monitoring capacity, a precondition the review's framework, built largely from higher-capacity settings, does not explicitly address. Two implications follow. First, establishing even minimal national shortage surveillance -Libya's most fundamental gap -should be treated as a prerequisite for the review's other recommended strategies, not one item among many. In practice, this precondition works best as a staged sequence. The first step is facility-level baseline audits of medicine availability. The second extends those audits into routine tracking of a minimal essential-medicines list. Only once that baseline exists should the third step -integration into regional pooled-procurement safeguards -follow. Libya's existing facility-level surveys (Dyab et al., 2026, Elfituri et al., 2018) already amount to an ad hoc version of the first step, so formalizing and extending this baseline is a realistic near-term policy target. Second, Libya's history with regional pooled procurement, from the failed 1981-1982 consortium to the 2026 APPM consultations, suggests that group-procurement mechanisms require specific safeguards against the purchasing-pattern disruption the review documents. This history should inform how the current mechanism is implemented and evaluated. Two safeguards follow directly: flexible demand-forecasting arrangements through framework agreements with minimum-maximum volume bands and regional buffer stocks, so member states can adjust pooled order volumes as local consumption data come in rather than committing to fixed quantities in advance, and standardized supply-chain logistics protocols across participating countries. Both would address the purchasing-pattern disruptions the review documents ;the same disruptions that undermined the earlier consortium.Libya's fragmented but consistent evidence -facility-level surveys, procurement-system analysis, and a documented history of regional pooled-procurement engagement -both confirms the review's causal framework and exposes its practical limits: a conflict-affected, importdependent context with no domestic manufacturing base and no national surveillance system. In the absence of baseline shortage monitoring in countries like Libya, it is difficult to apply the recommendations formulated in such global strategies and guidelines. Bridging this evidence gap-beginning with basic shortage monitoring-is a necessary precondition for adapting and translating the review's recommendations into meaningful action in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

title: Functional and Adverse-Event Outcomes Two to Three Years After Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Inpatient Care in Japan: Associations with Adverse Childhood Experiences
abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are prevalent among psychiatrically hospitalized youth, but their long-term associations are poorly characterized outside Western settings. This retrospective cohort study extended a one-year outcome study from a Japanese child and adolescent psychiatric inpatient unit to two-to-three years post-discharge (N = 106; medical-protection admissions, 2021–2024), with ACE exposure assessed at discharge by multidisciplinary consensus. Higher ACE burden was independently associated with longer length of stay and greater odds of seclusion and physical restraint, reproducing the index study. The longitudinal CGAS effect was nonsignificant, and the ACE–CGAS correlation attenuated from admission to 24 months. A composite adverse outcome increased with ACE burden (14.8% at ACE = 0 versus 51.1% at ACE ≥ 4; adjusted OR = 1.37, 95% CI 1.15–1.64), but 24-month retention also differed by ACE group (89% versus 60%), so this functional attenuation must be interpreted alongside differential attrition.

title: From Lumbar Puncture to Pseudo-Fever: Diagnostic Cascades and Delayed Recognition of Psychosomatic Origins in Pediatric Fever of Unknown Origin
abstract: Objective Pediatric fever of unknown origin (FUO) routinely triggers an infectious diagnostic cascade—laboratory testing, imaging, lumbar puncture (LP), bone marrow aspiration (BMA), and empiric antibiotics—before non-infectious etiologies are considered. This retrospective study quantifies the diagnostic intensity and healthcare resource utilization among hospitalized children with FUO ultimately suspected of having psychosomatic origins, and identifies opportunities for earlier multidisciplinary recognition. Methods Medical records of 80 hospitalized children aged 9–13 years (January 2023–January 2026) admitted for fever ≥ 37.5°C with negative infectious workups and eventual documentation of suspected conversion disorder or “pseudo-fever” were reviewed. Variables included invasive procedures, antibiotic exposure, diagnostic certainty at discharge, length of stay (LOS), and discharge outcomes. Categorical data were analyzed using chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Results The cohort comprised 80 children (44 females, 55.0%; 36 males, 45.0%), with 67.5% aged 12–13 years. Before psychosomatic etiology was suspected, 30.0% underwent LP, 22.5% underwent BMA, and 95.0% received intravenous antibiotics. Median LOS was 12 days (IQR: 8–18). Only 40.0% received a definitive psychiatric diagnosis at discharge; 60.0% remained tentative. “Pseudo-fever” was documented in 58.8% of cases. Discharge outcomes were cured (25.0%), improved (62.5%), and unfavorable (12.5%). In exploratory analysis, females had higher cure rates (36.4% vs. 11.1%, p = 0.021), while males had more unfavorable outcomes (25.0% vs. 2.3%, p = 0.003). Conclusions Children with FUO ultimately suspected of psychosomatic etiology undergo substantial invasive testing and antibiotic exposure before psychiatric evaluation. These data support implementing early multidisciplinary pediatric–psychiatry pathways and standardized psychosomatic screening within 48–72 hours of admission when initial infectious workups return negative, to reduce unnecessary procedures and shorten diagnostic delay.
