title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models
abstract: Clinical data are split across incomplete cohorts with partially overlapping variables. Causal discovery under missing data and multi-source integration have developed separately, and tabular foundation models cannot take a causal graph without retraining. We make two contributions. First, causal graph fusion learns a partial ancestral graph on the shared variables, fuses it into each cohort's graph under temporal background knowledge and lets Markov blankets guide re-imputation, so missing data are handled inside discovery. Second, causal attention steering compiles the learned graph into the attention of a frozen tabular foundation model at inference. Against known ground truth, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001), and steering improves discrimination under distribution shift (p<10-5), a gain that a random graph does not produce. In two spinal cord injury cohorts, fusion orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set no single cohort orients in full, and yields compact, temporally ordered predictor sets that match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes.

title: Urban Primary Healthcare Purchasing in Bangladesh: Analysis of Current Arrangements, Governance Structures and Policy Landscape
abstract: Bangladesh's urban primary healthcare (PHC) system faces governance fragmentation between Ministry of Health and Ministry of Local Government, with limited public provision and heavy reliance on donor-funded programmes delivered through private and NGO providers. Strategic purchasing is considered for potentially improving efficiency and quality, yet transitioning to this approach requires baseline understanding of current operational arrangements and mechanisms. This study examines purchasing arrangements in Bangladesh's urban PHC system, including contracting and funding modalities, and identifies their strengths and challenges. This qualitative study employed desk-based document review, 32 key informant interviews with national and city-level stakeholders, and two stakeholder validation workshops. Purposive sampling included policymakers from government ministries, local government officials, development partners, NGO project managers, and academics. Thematic analysis followed a hybrid approach combining deductive coding against WHO health system building blocks and inductive coding for emergent themes. The analysis identified four major urban PHC models predominantly delivered through public-private partnerships. Key challenges include procurement regulations that lacked provisions for healthcare services until Public Procurement Ordinance 2025 reforms, input-oriented rather than outcome-based contracting, emphasizing cost-saving over quality, governance disconnect where local government institutions hold responsibility but lack technical expertise and financial authority, chronic human resource and capacity constraints, and donor-dependency undermining sustainability. Population health needs assessment was notably absent from purchasing decisions. Recent regulatory reforms provide a legal foundation for strategic purchasing, but our findings indicate it cannot be introduced as a single reform. Successful transition requires institutional resolution of governance fragmentation, sustainable domestic financing mechanisms replacing project-based approaches, and systematic institutional capacity building in contract management and stewardship.

title: Challenges and opportunities in the Arab pharmaceutical sector: a multidimensional review toward self-sufficiency
abstract: Background Pharmaceutical self-sufficiency depends on interacting scientific, industrial and institutional capabilities. This review examines their implications for medicine access in Arab countries. Methods A structured critical narrative approach combines empirical studies, previous reviews and official guidance. A targeted PubMed search executed on 8 September 2026 retrieved 331 unique records, from which 19 empirical publications were purposively retained after a focused reassessment of four existing records, and a documented OpenAlex extension supported positioning against previous reviews. The original screening and 121 appraisal judgments underwent the reported human procedures; the authors also reviewed and approved the 34 additional judgments from the focused reassessment. Results Workforce studies from Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Lebanon and Qatar measure career preferences, employment destinations, self-assessed knowledge or competence and educational perceptions as separate outcomes; they cannot be combined into a regional industrial-employment estimate. Regulatory milestones, including participation of the Saudi and Jordanian authorities in the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S) and World Health Organization (WHO) maturity level 4 for Saudi Arabia, document institutional achievements that require function-specific evaluation. Shortage studies from Saudi Arabia, Lebanon and Sudan, together with the Egyptian hepatitis C case, show that production, pricing, procurement and distribution interact; the evidence does not identify any import-dependence level that predicts shortages. Biosimilars, devices, intellectual property, pharmacovigilance, digital technologies, environmental safeguards and research infrastructure are connected to these core capabilities. Observational designs, setting-specific samples and heterogeneous indicators constrain causal and regional inference. Conclusion Selective capacity development should be evaluated against medicine quality, affordability, availability and continuity. The proposed roadmap identifies responsibilities, resources and measurable decision criteria within illustrative planning horizons. The synthesis does not establish a common import-reduction target or demonstrate that domestic production alone improves access.

title: Simulation-based interprofessional education for the perioperative anaesthetic emergency team: a pre-post study within a multicentre trial
abstract: Background: Simulation is the most widely used strategy in interprofessional education (IPE), but it rarely involves the whole team that responds to crises, including support staff. This study explored, by professional category, how interprofessional collaborative competencies and knowledge changed after simulation with the perioperative anaesthetic emergency team. Methods: Pre-post study within a multicentre randomised trial that addressed two questions; the comparison between delivery settings is reported elsewhere, and the data were pooled here. Ninety-eight professionals (28 anaesthetists, 56 nurses and 14 healthcare assistants [HCAs]), in 14 teams of seven, took part in a standardised session on local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, with interprofessional PEARLS co-debriefing. The ICCAS and a knowledge questionnaire were administered before and after the session, the RIPLS before and the SET-M and DASH after. The facilitators' records were analysed post hoc. Results: No HCA had previously taken part in a simulation, compared with 89.3% of anaesthetists and 39.3% of nurses. Readiness for interprofessional learning (RIPLS) was highest in anaesthetists and lowest in HCAs (p < 0.001). ICCAS scores did not differ between categories at either time point. They increased in anaesthetists (68.75 ± 8.28 to 79.68 ± 9.88; p < 0.001) and nurses (69.43 ± 11.71 to 79.52 ± 12.44; p < 0.001), and the change was inconclusive in HCAs (72.79 ± 19.95 to 77.50 ± 19.52; p = 0.382), although 9 of the 14 reported on the global item that they collaborated better. Knowledge increased in all categories and DASH scores were similar. On the SET-M, HCAs rated learning and debriefing less favourably. All teams called for help early and redistributed tasks, but closed-loop communication was not always performed. Conclusions: Training the perioperative anaesthetic emergency team in an interprofessional intervention built to the Sim-IPE standard was feasible. The session was associated with higher self-reported collaborative competency in clinical professionals, and observation identified closed-loop communication as the team competency to strengthen. In HCAs, IPE instruments did not capture the change they themselves reported. The study extends simulation-based IPE beyond the doctor-nurse dyad, and future evaluation should include observed performance and follow-up. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07346937. Registered 10 December 2025.

title: Implications of delayed follow-up in pediatric post-discharge mortality research
abstract: The primary objective of this analysis was to explore the characteristics of participants who we had difficulty following up within a cohort with minimal follow-up losses, and to assess the impact this difficulty had on post-discharge mortality. This secondary analysis was conducted using data from a prospective, observational cohort study of children under five who were admitted with suspected sepsis at six hospitals in Uganda. Participants’ vital status was assessed through follow-up contact during three 2-month periods over a 6-month post-discharge observation time frame. For each period, follow-up difficulty was individually classified as “on-time” or “delayed”. Follow-up was classified as “delayed” if completed more than 60 days after the scheduled contact; follow up within 60 days was considered “on-time”. Logistic regression identified factors associated with follow-up difficulty, while Cox proportional hazard models evaluated the impact of follow-up difficulty on mortality and readmission. After being classified for difficulty across the three follow-up periods, 17,951 person-periods of observation were included. Of these, 3,392 (18.9%) were classified as delayed, and 14,559 (81.1%) were classified as on-time. Factors associated with delayed follow-up included malnutrition, HIV, respiratory distress, abnormal coma scale, low maternal education, long travel times, and unplanned discharge. Delayed follow-up did not significantly impact post-discharge mortality but reduced the likelihood of first readmission. Follow-up difficulty was common among children discharged from hospitals, particularly among socially vulnerable families but did not significantly impact post-discharge mortality. However, delayed follow-up was associated with reduced hospital readmission, possibly reflecting suboptimal care-seeking behaviour in these families.

title: Smart discharges and post-discharge mortality among children with suspected sepsis in Uganda: a prospective before-after study
abstract: Introduction Post-discharge mortality among children following an acute illness in low-resource settings is high and demands urgent attention. We aimed to assess the impact of Smart Discharges, a mortality prevention risk-differentiated approach to peri-discharge care among children under five years admitted with suspected sepsis. Methods We conducted a before-and-after two-phase study with staggered implementation at six hospitals in Uganda. During a baseline period (Phase-1), clinical prediction algorithms for post-discharge mortality were developed using clinical and sociodemographic data collected at hospital admission. Outcomes, primarily mortality within six months of discharge, were compared against an interventional period (Phase-2). In both phases, families were given soap and a mosquito net as compensation for participating. In the Smart Discharges intervention, each family also received their risk category (low/medium/high/very high), counselling, and educational materials, regardless of risk stratification, after which the intensity of recommended follow-up care was determined by age (0–6, 6–60 months) and predicted post-discharge mortality risk. Results Outcome data from 13,051 children were analyzed: Phase-1, n = 6,955; Phase-2, n = 6,096. Characteristics were generally similar between groups, including the mean predicted post-discharge mortality risk (6.3% in Phase-1 vs. 5.9% in Phase-2). With Smart Discharges, 2,337/3,892 (60.0%) medium/high/very high-risk families attended all their scheduled visits. The observed post-discharge mortality rate was 439 (6.3%) in Phase-1 vs. 296 (4.9%) in Phase-2; this represents an unadjusted absolute risk reduction of 1.4% (95%CI 0.7 to 2.3) and an adjusted hazard ratio 0.77 (95%CI 0.67 to 0.90) favouring the intervention. In Phase-1, 1,313 (18.9%) children were re-admitted to the hospital vs. 1,024 (16.8%) in Phase-2. Conclusion In this non-randomized, observational study, we found evidence that a simple risk assessment approach, paired with education and engagement through scheduled follow-up after discharge, may be an appropriate strategy to improve child survival in low-resource settings.

title: AI and IoT for Nurse Workload & Shift Management
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Nurses are the backbone of hospitals, but in India one nurse has to handle 20-30 patients due to shortage of 2 million nurses. Manual shift management on paper causes unfair duty, overtime, heavy paper work and burnout. 60% of nurses suffer from burnout and 40% leave job within 3 years, which increases patient risk and medication errors. This paper proposes a low-cost AI and IoT based Smart Nurse Workload & Shift Management System. The system uses ESP32 with smart wristband (MAX30102 for heart rate / SpO2, DS18B20 for temperature, MPU6050 for fall detection), bed sensor, RFID badge for nurse location, DHT11 for room monitoring, and cloud AI engine. AI calculates Patient Load Score - Critical = 3, Moderate = 2, Stable = 1, and auto-creates fair shift roster in 2 minutes considering patient load, nurse skill, fatigue and leave. It allocates tasks dynamically to nearest free nurse with lowest workload, auto-records vitals to reduce paper work, and predicts burnout risk if nurse works > 48 hours/week. System was tested in 2 hospitals and 1 old-age home for 30 days with 30 nurses, 120 patients and 900 shifts. Results show shift roster time reduced from 2 days to 2 minutes, burnout reduced from 60% to 22%, emergency response time reduced from 8 minutes to 2 minutes, medication errors reduced by 75%, patient satisfaction increased from 58% to 94%, and nurse satisfaction increased from 45% to 92%. AI achieved 91% accuracy in shift fairness, 87% in burnout prediction and 94% in vital monitoring. Cost per ward is only Rs. 15,000, making it suitable for government and private hospitals in India.

title: AI-Based Nurse Call & Patient Assistance System
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In hospitals, timely assistance from nurses is critical for patient safety and satisfaction. However, traditional nurse call systems using only a wired bell only indicate that a patient has called, but do not tell what the patient needs or how urgent it is. This leads to delay in response, increased nurse workload, and risk for emergency patients, especially elderly, paralyzed, and ICU patients who cannot press a button or speak. This paper proposes a low-cost, AI-based Nurse Call & Patient Assistance System using IoT and Artificial Intelligence. The system uses ESP32 microcontroller at each patient bed with call button, voice microphone (INMP441), speaker, MPU6050 for fall detection, MAX30102 for heart rate and SpO2, and PIR sensor for bed occupancy. Patient can call nurse by three ways - Button Press, Voice Command in Hindi, English and Marathi, or Automatic Call on fall / abnormal vitals. The voice is processed by AI Natural Language Processing (NLP) to understand intent - Water, Medicine, Washroom, Pain, Emergency, Doctor, and Machine Learning model classifies priority as Green (Normal), Yellow (Urgent), Red (Emergency). The system then assigns the nearest available nurse and sends instant notification to nurse mobile app and smartwatch with Bed No, Room No, Patient Name and Need. If nurse does not accept within 2 minutes, system auto-escalates to next nurse and Head Nurse. The system was tested on 10 beds with 50 patients for 15 days. It achieved 91% accuracy in voice intent recognition, 93% accuracy in priority classification, and 95% accuracy in fall detection. Average nurse response time reduced from 8-10 minutes to 1 min 42 sec, nurse workload reduced by 30%, and patient satisfaction increased from 62% to 94%. Cost per bed is only Rs. 2,500, making it suitable for small hospitals, rural PHCs, ICU, elderly care and old-age homes.

title: Delayed Transperineal Anastomotic Urethroplasty for Pediatric Pelvic Fracture Urethral Injury: Feasibility and Early Outcomes of a Prospective Cohort Study
Environmental influences and implementation effectiveness of community-based hypertension management: a five-year natural experiment in Southwest China
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypertension management poses significant challenges in regions experiencing rapid urbanization, particularly where healthcare resources vary substantially across urban and rural areas. Luzhou City's community-based hypertension management program, initiated in 2014 and gradually expanded city-wide, provides valuable insights into implementing chronic disease management in diverse socioeconomic settings. This study evaluates the program's effectiveness through a five-year natural experiment, examining detection rates, implementation patterns, and environmental and socioeconomic influences. METHODS: We analyzed health examination data from seven districts and counties of Luzhou City (2019-2023), encompassing 122 townships and streets. Environmental data, including air pollutants, vegetation coverage, and meteorological parameters, were obtained from the Weijing Remote Sensing platform and National Tibetan Plateau Data Center. Spatial autocorrelation analysis and Bayesian spatiotemporal modeling were employed to assess program implementation patterns and environmental and socioeconomic influences on detection rates. Regular calibration of equipment and standardized training of healthcare providers ensured data quality. RESULTS: City-wide hypertension detection rates increased from 21.60% in 2019 to 29.27% in 2023, with notable regional variations. Less economically developed counties demonstrated exceptional improvements, with Gulin and Luxian achieving the highest annual improvement rates (Estimated Annual Percentage Change [EAPC]: 10.57% and 10.22%, respectively). Middle-aged adults (45-49 years) showed the most substantial improvement (EAPC: 14.45%). Bayesian spatiotemporal modeling identified significant environmental and socioeconomic correlates: average temperature showed the strongest environmental association (RR = 1.0506 per 1 °C, 95% CrI: 1.0186-1.0850), followed by O₃ concentration (RR = 1.0224 per 1 µg/m³, 95% CrI: 1.0158-1.0314). GDP and urbanization rate were negatively associated with detection rates, while hospital bed density showed a positive association (RR = 1.0314 per 1 bed/1,000 population, 95% CrI: 1.0155-1.0521). Spatial analysis revealed persistent clustering patterns (Moran's I: 0.1889-0.2655, P < 0.05), indicating structural influences on program effectiveness. CONCLUSIONS: The successful implementation of community-based hypertension management in resource-limited settings demonstrates the feasibility of reducing healthcare disparities through systematic approaches. The varying effectiveness across regions and age groups, coupled with significant environmental influences, indicates the importance of context-sensitive implementation strategies. These findings provide valuable guidance for chronic disease management in developing regions, emphasizing the potential for achieving health equity through well-structured community health programs. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Financial efficiency of Bhayangkara Hospitals as public service agencies: A two-stage DEA–Tobit analysis
journal: Jurnal Tata Kelola dan Akuntabilitas Keuangan Negara
abstract: Public hospitals operating under the Public Service Agency (Badan Layanan Umum, BLU) scheme are expected to manage financial resources efficiently while maintaining continuous public service delivery. This study analyzes the operational financial efficiency (OFE) of Bhayangkara Hospitals with BLU status and identifies factors associated with efficiency variation using a quantitative panel data approach for 40 hospitals from 2020 to 2024. Efficiency was measured using data envelopment analysis (DEA) with variable returns to scale and output orientation, employing personnel expenditure, goods expenditure, and capital expenditure as inputs and hospital revenue as output. The resulting efficiency scores are subsequently analyzed using a random-effects panel Tobit model. The DEA results reveal that most hospitals have not achieved full OFE, with only a few consistently operating on the efficiency frontier. Tobit regression indicates that average length of stay, number of supporting staff, number of physicians, and the COVID-19 period are significantly correlated with efficiency, while bed occupancy ratio, turnover interval, and nonphysician health personnel are not. This study provides an early empirical assessment of the financial efficiency of BLU Bhayangkara Hospitals and demonstrates the potential of a two-stage DEA–Tobit approach as a research-based audit tool for efficiency screening, benchmarking, and performance evaluation in public health sector audits.

title: Right ventricular assist device support during left ventricular assist device implantation: indications, timing, device selection, and perioperative management
abstract: Right heart failure (RHF) after implantation of a durable left ventricular assist device is a major clinical problem, but prediction of RHF, actual use of a right ventricular assist device (RVAD), and benefit from earlier RVAD support are distinct questions. This narrative review examines the evidence linking these questions and its limitations. Contemporary guidance supports serial clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive hemodynamic assessment; optimization of right ventricular (RV) loading; and consideration of temporary support for refractory failure. No single hemodynamic or risk-score threshold establishes a universal indication for a planned RVAD implantation. Retrospective studies, including HeartMate 3 cohorts, report associations between upfront support and better outcomes than rescue support; non-random allocation and evolving illness severity limit causal interpretation. We review the RV strain, three-dimensional imaging, RV–pulmonary artery coupling, and dynamic assessment and compare surgical RVAD, ProtekDuo, Impella RP and RP Flex, oxygenated RVAD, and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. An author-proposed decision pathway connects physiological assessment, correction of reversible causes, support selection, and reassessment of recovery. This pathway is not a validated treatment-allocation model. Furthermore, decisions require integration of reversibility, organ perfusion, oxygenation, anticipated support duration, transplant eligibility, and local expertise. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether risk-informed RVAD strategies improve patient outcomes.

title: Bilateral chronic subdural hematomas in a five-year-old boy with previous meningitis and no history of trauma: a case report
journal: The Egyptian Journal of Neurosurgery : the official publication of the Egyptian Society of Neurological Surgeons/Egyptian journal of neurosurgery
abstract: Background Chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) is uncommon in children. Pediatric CSDH has been associated with trauma, child abuse, coagulation abnormalities, cerebrospinal fluid shunting, and other underlying conditions. We report a five-year-old boy with large bilateral chronic subdural hematomas, a previous history of meningitis, and no history of trauma. Case presentation A five-year-old boy presented with approximately two months of impaired consciousness, recurrent episodes of focal seizures, and spasticity involving the limbs. He had a previous history of meningitis but no history of trauma or developmental delay. On admission, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 9/15. Both pupils were mid-sized and sluggishly reactive to light. Brain CT demonstrated large bilateral frontoparietotemporal subdural collections measuring approximately 31 mm on the left and 22 mm on the right, with significant mass effect on the underlying cerebral parenchyma. The collections were radiologically considered chronic subdural hematomas. The patient underwent bilateral surgical evacuation. A left-sided craniotomy was performed with evacuation of the chronic subdural hematoma and excision of a double-layered subdural capsule. The right-sided collection was evacuated through a burr hole. No specimen was submitted for histopathological examination. Following surgery, the focal seizures ceased, limb spasticity improved, and the patient’s GCS improved from 9/15 to 13/15 at discharge. Postoperative CT demonstrated marked reduction of the bilateral subdural collections. Conclusion Large bilateral chronic subdural hematomas should be considered in children presenting with prolonged impaired consciousness, focal seizures, and spasticity, even in the absence of trauma. Previous meningitis may represent a possible predisposing factor, although causality could not be established in this case. Surgical evacuation, including membranectomy of the organized left- sided collection, was followed by substantial neurological improvement.

title: Confirmation of Sengstaken-Blakemore Tube Placement Using POCUS During Life-Threatening Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed: A Case Report
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
abstract: Introduction: Acute gastroesophageal variceal hemorrhage is a life-threatening emergency requiring rapid hemostasis. Sengstaken-Blakemore tube placement remains an important temporizing intervention in patients with refractory bleeding; however, improper positioning, particularly inflation of the gastric balloon within the esophagus, can result in catastrophic complications including esophageal rupture. Radiographic confirmation is traditionally recommended but may delay intervention in unstable patients. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has emerged as a potential alternative for real-time confirmation of balloon placement. Our case demonstrates how POCUS can be used to rapidly and safely confirm intragastric Sengstaken-Blakemore tube placement prior to balloon inflation in an unstable patient with massive variceal hemorrhage and hemorrhagic shock. Case Report: We describe a 62-year-old woman with severe alcohol use disorder who presented with massive hematemesis and hemorrhagic shock. Despite administration of ceftriaxone, octreotide, pantoprazole, vasopressors, and activation of massive transfusion protocol, the patient remained hemodynamically unstable with ongoing large-volume hematemesis. After endotracheal intubation, a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube was placed. Point-of-care ultrasound using a curvilinear probe was performed prior to full balloon inflation, demonstrating the gastric balloon within the stomach through dynamic visualization of balloon movement and intragastric air. Following confirmation, the gastric balloon was fully inflated and traction applied, resulting in effective tamponade and improved hemodynamics. Subsequent endoscopy confirmed bleeding esophageal and gastroesophageal varices, which were successfully banded, and the patient was ultimately discharged from the hospital. Conclusion: Point-of-care ultrasound is a tool that can be rapidly employed at the bedside to confirm intragastric placement of Sengstaken-Blakemore tubes, potentially improving time to tamponade and minimizing the risk of catastrophic malposition-related complications in patients with massive variceal hemorrhage.

title: Experiences of Families of Patients Admitted in Intensive Care Unit at a Faith Based Referral Hospital, Kenya: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
journal: Journal of Clinical Care and Medical Advancement
abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admissions and bed capacity have increased with rising critical illness, improved infrastructure and resource allocation. Sudden, life-threatening admissions strain families emotionally, financially and psychologically, yet few Kenyan studies guide family support. This study explored the emotional, physical and psychological responses, communication experiences, socioeconomic burden and coping strategies of family members of patients in an adult ICU in a tertiary hospital in Kenya. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted from October to November 2025 in the five -bed adult ICU of a faith-based referral hospital in Kiambu County, Kenya. Twelve family members (N=12) from 10 families were purposively recruited. We audio-recorded and transcribed semi-structured interviews (30-60 minutes, in English or Kiswahili), then analysed them using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. Sample adequacy was evaluated using Malterud’s information power framework. Four themes emerged. First, emotional, physical, and psychological turmoil, marked by widespread fear, anxiety, and viewing the ICU as a place of death. Second, a communication and information gap: inaccessible clinicians, inconsistent updates, and one participant’s perception of culturally insensitive communication by a foreign clinician. Third, socioeconomic burden: high bills and debt despite having health insurance, fear of detention over unpaid bills, and livelihood disruption. Fourth, coping strategies: spiritual faith and prayer, family role adaptation and informal social networks, whose support waned over time. Families experienced emotional, physical and psychological turmoil, communication gaps and substantial socioeconomic burden despite all having health insurance. Spiritual faith, family role adaptation and informal networks were the coping strategies described, although network support waned. Structured multi-professional communication, spiritual and psychosocial support for families who want it, and a review of insurance cover for ICU costs are recommended.

title: A novel microbeam radiosurgery treatment for intractable seizures utilizing tissue-sparing 25- to 50-μm synchrotron-derived x-rays
An Integrated Explainable COD and BOD Predictive Modeling Framework for Oxygen Uptake Rate Estimation and Feedforward PI Aeration Control in Municipal Wastewater Treatment Plants
abstract: The aeration process in an activated sludge wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) is the most energy-demanding process, consuming about 45–60% of the total energy consumption. Most traditional dissolved oxygen (DO) control methods rely on a feedback proportional–integral (PI) controller, which responds only after a disturbance affects the biological process and may lead to delayed response, excessive aeration, and higher energy consumption. Accurate prediction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and biological oxygen demand (BOD) offers a chance to manage aeration proactively. Laboratory COD and BOD tests are laborious and time-consuming and cannot be implemented for online operation, which challenges real-time process optimization. This research study proposes an integrated framework that combines predictive models with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), oxygen uptake rate (OUR) estimation, and feedforward (FF) PI aeration control for a municipal WWTP. Based on the proposed method, we compare Atrous Neural Network (Atrous NN), artificial neural network (ANN), and random forest (RF) models for COD and BOD prediction and then use the predicted values of the best model for OUR estimation, which gives an FF signal together with a PI controller to control the DO response. The predictive models were developed and evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). The comparative analysis showed that the Atrous NN model exhibited the best predictive ability, with R2 values of 0.9941 and 0.9868 and RMSE of 0.4397 and 0.2285 and MAE of 0.3413 and 0.1797 for COD and BOD, respectively, showing good correlation between predicted and measured values. Additionally, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed that Nitro-Ratio, TSS-Nitro-Ratio, and Madiwala STP-avg-TSS interaction were identified as the most important features influencing model performance. Consequently, five DO control architectures, i.e., PI-Only control, FF-Only control, FF(COD) + PI control, FF(BOD) + PI control, and FF(COD + BOD) + PI control, were also developed and evaluated using rise time (RT), settling time (ST), peak time (PT), percentage overshoot (%OS), steady-state error (SSE), Integral Absolute Error (IAE), Integral Squared Error (ISE), and Integral Time Absolute Error (ITAE). The results obtained show that the FF(COD + BOD) + PI control strategy achieved the best performance among the rest, with the lowest RT (146s), ST (1292s), PT (11832s), %OS (0.93), SSE (0.00), IAE (534), and ISE (759). Furthermore, the power and energy analyses showed that the FF(COD + BOD) + PI control strategy achieved the highest energy reduction rate of 13.69%. However, the estimated decrease in aeration energy consumption is a theoretical improvement in simulated control performance, as the effluent concentrations of COD, BOD, and NH-N were not evaluated. Hence, experimental validation is required to verify the effectiveness of the treatment and meet the relevant statutory discharge restrictions.

title: Management of Advanced Uterovaginal Prolapse Under Local Anesthesia in a Patient with Complete Atrioventricular Block
abstract: Advanced pelvic organ prolapse can cause significant urinary and bowel dysfunction. Coexisting complete atrioventricular (AV) block with unavailability of temporary and permanent pacing poses significant perioperative anesthetic challenges. Our case involves a 70-year-old para 8 woman who presented with stage 4 uterovaginal prolapse complicated by difficulty defecating and urinary retention. She also had complete atrioventricular block with a ventricular rate of approximately 38 beats per minute, mild valvular regurgitation, and bronchial asthma. Pacemaker insertion was financially unaffordable. Following multidisciplinary assessment and high-risk informed consent, partial LeFort colpocleisis with perineorrhaphy was performed under local anesthesia using lidocaine infiltration with minimal systemic analgesia and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. The patient was stable throughout surgery and postoperatively and was discharged without complications. This case highlights the challenges of perioperative decision-making and the potential role of individualized anesthetic planning in resource-limited settings.

title: Posttraumatic Pulsating Frontal Mass Lesion: A Vascular Pitfall
journal: Journal of Maxillofacial and Oral Surgery
abstract: Traumatic pseudoaneurysm of the superficial temporal artery (STA) is a rare but clinically relevant complication of blunt head trauma that may initially mimic a posttraumatic hematoma. We report a 75-year-old woman receiving low-dose aspirin who initially presented with a small left frontal hematoma after a fall. After local wound care, she was discharged. Fifteen days later, she re-presented with progressive pulsatile swelling in the left frontal region. Color-coded duplex ultrasonography demonstrated an approximately 18 × 14 mm perfused pseudoaneurysm sac with bidirectional flow and a directly visualized communicating neck to the frontal branch of the left STA. Open treatment consisted of proximal ligation and transection of the main STA trunk, followed by evacuation of the associated hematoma and pseudocapsule. During 12 months of clinical follow-up, no recurrent swelling, pulsation, or neurological impairment was reported. This case highlights that duplex ultrasonography should be considered early in persistent, pulsatile, or otherwise unclear post-traumatic forehead lesions and that management should be individualized according to lesion anatomy, symptoms, and patient-specific factors.

title: Correction: Adhesive small bowel obstruction in a 3-year-old child with history of necrotizing enterocolitis: a case report
abstract: Background and objectives: Adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) is a serious complication following abdominal surgery in children, yet its presenting symptoms often mimic non-surgical conditions such as viral mesenteric adenitis and functional constipation. This diagnostic challenge is particularly acute in young children with a history of neonatal intestinal surgery who cannot reliably communicate their symptoms. This case report describes a former extreme preterm infant with surgical history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) who presented with acute abdominal pain and was found to have complete mechanical small bowel obstruction due to postoperative adhesions. The objective is to highlight the diagnostic pitfalls in this population and to describe an unusual postoperative course complicated by three concurrent infections. Case presentation: A 3-year-7-month-old former preterm girl (23 weeks gestation) with a history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) requiring jejunal resection and stoma closure presented with one day of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation. Initial ultrasound showed reactive mesenteric lymph nodes and fecal loading, suggesting mesenteric adenitis and constipation. However, given her surgical history, she was admitted for observation. Abdominal x-ray revealed small bowel dilatation with air-fluid levels, and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed complete mechanical small bowel obstruction with pneumatosis intestinalis. She underwent emergent laparotomy, which revealed extensive adhesive bands causing obstruction without volvulus, and adhesiolysis was performed without complication. On postoperative day 17, she developed a one-day fever. Workup revealed three concurrent infections: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, adenovirus, and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar. She was treated with intravenous meropenem and metronidazole and recovered fully. Conclusion: Children with prior intestinal surgery can present with acute abdominal pain that mimics non-surgical conditions such as mesenteric adenitis and constipation while having a complete adhesive small bowel obstruction requiring emergent surgery. Normal or equivocal ultrasound findings do not exclude this diagnosis, and a low threshold for CT is essential. Postoperative fever in such patients warrants a broad infectious workup, as multiple concurrent pathogens may coexist.Adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)is a common and potentially life-threatening complication following abdominal surgery in children (1). The formation of fibrous bands between loops of intestine, known as adhesions, occurs in virtually all patients after peritoneal injury, though only a subset develops clinically significant obstruction (2). Adhesions typically form within the first month after surgery as part of the normal peritoneal healing response, but their pathological progression into symptomatic obstruction can take months or even years to manifest, and obstruction can occur suddenly without prior warning symptoms (3). In the pediatric population, the incidence of adhesive obstruction following laparotomy ranges from 5% to 25%, with the highest risk observed in neonates who undergo intestinal surgery for conditions such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), intestinal atresia, or gastroschisis (4,5).The diagnosis of Adhesive small bowel obstruction in young children presents unique challenges. Presenting symptoms, abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and abdominal distension, are non-specific and overlap substantially with far more common non-surgical conditions such as viral gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, and functional constipation (2). Young children, particularly those of preschool age, cannot reliably articulate the quality, location, or severity of their pain, nor can they provide a detailed history of associated symptoms. This reliance on parental observation and physical examination alone introduces significant uncertainty into the diagnostic process (6). In a child with prior laparotomy, the consequences of missing an adhesive obstruction are severe, as delayed diagnosis can lead to bowel ischemia, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and death (7). This diagnostic dilemma is further complicated by the radiation exposure associated with computed tomography (CT) in young children and the difficulty of performing serial abdominal examinations in a distressed or uncooperative child (7,8).This case is noteworthy because it involves a child with a complex surgical history in whom the initial presentation mimicked non-surgical conditions, creating a diagnostic challenge with potentially serious consequences. Additionally, the postoperative course revealed an unusual combination of concurrent infections that are rarely described together in the literature. This report aims to describe the successful management of this complex case and to provide practical lessons for clinicians evaluating children with prior abdominal surgery who present with acute abdominal pain.A 3-year-7-month-old girl presented to the emergency department with a one-hour history of severe diffuse abdominal pain. According to her mother, the child had been constipated for the preceding two days but had eaten her breakfast normally and then began complaining of intense pain. The mother observed that the child attempted to have a bowel movement without success, and the pain worsened with straining. The child was noted to be curling her body in response to the pain, a posture consistent with significant intra-abdominal discomfort. There was no associated vomiting at the time of initial presentation, no fever, and no urinary symptoms. The initial emergency department examination revealed a well-appearing, alert child with stable vital signs, but there was notable abdominal guarding such that she cried when the abdomen was palpated. Based on these findings, the decision was made to transfer the patient via ambulance to another hospital for further evaluation.Upon arrival at the hospital later that same day, the history was further elaborated. The child had experienced central to epigastric colicky abdominal pain that was non-radiating and had been ongoing for approximately 24 h. One episode of vomiting had occurred. The mother reported that the child had not passed stool on the day of presentation and had decreased oral intake. There was a history of runny nose approximately one week prior to presentation, suggesting a possible preceding viral illness. Review of systems was otherwise negative for diarrhea and urinary frequency or dysuria. The patient's past medical history was remarkable for prematurity at 23 weeks gestation, with a birth weight of 435 grams, complicated by respiratory distress syndrome, persistent pulmonary hypertension, recurrent left pneumothorax, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and patent ductus arteriosus that closed with paracetamol therapy. Most significantly, she developed NEC on day 52 of life requiring laparotomy with resection of 20 cm of jejunum and creation of a jejunostomy. By postoperative day 17, the stoma was successfully closed and she tolerated full oral feeding. Additional past medical history included anemia of prematurity which was resolved, borderline thyroid function tests that normalized, periventricular leukomalacia on neonatal brain ultrasound, mild speech delay, and no evidence of adrenal insufficiency. She had no hospitalizations since NICU discharge, and she was not on any regular medications at the time of presentation. Allergies included moderate reactions to beef and cow's milk, both manifesting as itching.Physical examination on admission to the hospital revealed an ill-appearing child in apparent pain with signs of mild dehydration. Vital signs were stable with heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation within normal limits for age. Throat examination showed congestion. Chest auscultation revealed clear breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes or crackles. Abdominal examination was notable for soft but tender abdomen, with tenderness localized to the central and lower abdomen. Importantly, there was no right iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no rebound tenderness, and bowel sounds were present. However, given the child's high-risk surgical history, the clinical team proceeded with admission for observation and serial abdominal examinations rather than discharge.The initial diagnostic workup included laboratory studies and abdominal ultrasound. Serum C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 7 mg/L, a non-specific finding that could be consistent with either an inflammatory or infectious process.A complete blood count obtained on the day of admission showed a white blood cell count of 3.94 × 10 3 /μL, which is below the normal range of for age. The differential revealed 65.5% neutrophils, 28.2% lymphocytes (low), and 6.3% monocytes, with eosinophils and basophils at 0%. Hemoglobin was 13.2 g/dL (within normal range) and platelet count was 267 × 10 3 /μL (normal). Subsequent CRP monitoring showed a progressive rise to 42.2 mg/L, 126 mg/L, and 106 mg/L.Abdominal ultrasound performed on the day of admission was limited due to a gassy abdomen and fecal material, which are wellrecognized factors that reduce the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound for bowel obstruction, but it revealed multiple hypoechoic periumbilical and right lower quadrant lymph nodes, the largest measuring 1.8 cm, which were interpreted as likely reactive. The appendix was not visualized. There was no free fluid or localized collection. The liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys were all unremarkable. The bladder was underfilled but appeared unremarkable. Based on these ultrasound findings combined with the history of constipation, the initial assessment was acute abdominal pain likely secondary to mesenteric adenitis and constipation with fecal loading. However, the clinical team explicitly noted that given the patient's past surgical history of NEC with bowel resection, it was necessary to exclude an evolving surgical abdomen or pancreatitis.The diagnostic turning point occurred when abdominal x-rays (supine and erect views) were obtained. The radiographs demonstrated few air-fluid levels in the mid abdomen and pelvis associated with small bowel dilatation measuring up to 3.5 cm in diameter. Additionally, a "peak sign" and abrupt obstruction of mid-abdomen small bowel loops were noted, findings highly suggestive of bowel obstruction, possibly due to volvulus. No pneumoperitoneum was observed. In response to these concerning findings, the surgical team was consulted, and a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast was performed emergently. The CT scan confirmed mechanical complete small bowel obstruction. Small bowel loops were dilated to 3 cm in maximum diameter, and large bowel loops were dilated to 3.7 cm. More concerningly, the scan demonstrated wall edema of the rectum and sigmoid loops with air within the bowel wall, pneumatosis intestinalis, causing proximal dilatation of the large bowel. Rotating superior mesenteric vessels at the mid jejunal level and an adhesion band within jejunal loops with areas of narrowing were seen, suggestive of either volvulus or post-surgical adhesions. The impression was mechanical complete small bowel obstruction due to volvulus or adhesions, with pneumatosis intestinalis of the rectosigmoid colon. The surgical team was immediately notified.Following confirmation of complete small bowel obstruction, the patient was kept NPO (nil per os), intravenous fluids (D5% normal saline at 50 mL/hr) were continued, and she was prepared for emergency surgery. A chest x-ray obtained prior to surgery showed bilateral subtle granular opacities with rightsided predominance and mild pleural effusion, findings suggestive of an inflammatory or infectious process, though the patient was afebrile at that time. Intraoperative findings included extensive small bowel adhesions and multiple adhesive bands causing obstruction (Figure 1). The surgeon performed extensive small bowel adhesiolysis, excision of multiple bands, and an incidental appendectomy. The procedure was completed without complication and with minimal blood loss as documented by the operating surgeon. There was no volvulus identified intraoperatively; the obstruction was purely adhesive in nature. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the surgical ward for postoperative care.On the first postoperative day, the patient was hemodynamically stable and appeared well, not in pain or distress. Her vital signs remained within acceptable parameters. The abdomen was soft but not fully examinable due to the fresh surgical site. She was maintained NPO with intravenous D5% normal saline and received regular paracetamol 170 mg intravenously every six hours as needed for pain control. The surgical team ordered monitoring of complete blood count and electrolytes, and they planned to follow the pediatric surgery plan closely.By postoperative day three, the patient showed significant clinical improvement. Abdominal distention had decreased, she had not vomited, she was ambulating, and she had been started on an oral soft diet. She was passing urine freely and regularly, and she had passed a moderate amount of more watery stool once during the night and once in the morning. She was receiving oral high-energy nutritional supplement, oral rehydration solution, intravenous fluids with potassium chloride, and oral macrogol for constipation prevention. The abdominal examination at this time showed a mobile abdomen with respiration, very mild distension, a clean dry and intact surgical wound, a soft abdomen, and audible bowel sounds on auscultation.The postoperative course was complicated by a one-day fever along with persistent abdominal distension that had been noted since the surgery. The viral respiratory panel returned positive for adenovirus. Urine culture grew extended-spectrum betalactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli, establishing the diagnosis of a urinary tract infection with a multidrug-resistant organism. Stool analysis revealed the presence of Entamoeba histolytica/dispar cysts and trophozoites, indicating possible intestinal amebiasis. The stool analysis also showed greenish, mucoid consistency with 7 pus cells and 2 + mucus. By the time these results were available, the patient's fever had resolved spontaneously. She had started oral intake without vomiting and had passed stool. Her vital signs were stable. The physical examination documented a soft abdomen with distention, normal bowel sounds, and no guarding.The treatment plan, as approved by the pediatric consultant, consisted of intravenous meropenem at 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 h (215 mg three times daily) for the ESBL E. coli urinary tract infection, combined with intravenous metronidazole for a total of 5 days to cover both anaerobic bacteria and the Entamoeba infection. The patient was encouraged to take oral intake gradually as tolerated. No specific antiviral therapy was administered for adenovirus. By the time of discharge, the patient had recovered fully, tolerating an oral diet, passing stool Frontiers in Surgery 04 frontiersin.org regularly, and afebrile off antibiotics. She was discharged home with outpatient follow-up arranged with both the surgery and pediatrics teams.This case describes a former preterm infant with surgical history of necrotizing enterocolitis who presented with acute abdominal pain mimicking mesenteric adenitis and constipation, but was found to have complete ASBO requiring adhesiolysis, complicated postoperatively by three concurrent infections. title: Mechanism-based clinical reasoning in anesthesiology education: instructional design, assessment and learning transfer
abstract: Mechanism-based clinical reasoning may help anesthesiology learners connect physiological explanations with predictions and management decisions, but its educational effectiveness remains uncertain. This critical narrative review examines instructional features, assessment, and transfer while separating direct anesthesia education from indirect evidence and author proposals. The original purposive selection was supplemented by five documented database queries on 23 September 2026; a 1 January 2000–23 September 2026 analytic subset of those archived exports comprised 250 retrievals and 180 unique records. Thirty-five learner-outcome reports were retained, with eight previously identified reports added. The 43-report evidence inventory comprises 12 direct anesthesia education reports, seven anesthesia-adjacent reports, and 24 reports from other health-professions settings. Appraisal identifies cohort confounding, additional instructional exposure, incomplete follow-up, local outcome measures, and limited transfer testing. Favorable knowledge, satisfaction, or explanation scores do not consistently coincide with better reasoning performance. Indirect experiments support testing explicit causal connections and comparison across cases, but cannot establish benefit in perioperative management. We present an unvalidated six-part action cycle as an organization of existing reasoning principles, rather than a new theory or a superior teaching model. An accompanying unvalidated assessment blueprint separates mechanistic explanations, decision quality, retention, transfer, and preparation for future learning, with safety errors recorded independently. Prospective studies should use adequately resourced comparators, validated outcome interpretations, blinded assessment, delayed testing, and prespecified transfer tasks before claims of improved clinical reasoning or adaptive expertise are made.

title: How to choose the best surgical hospital in Bangalore?

abstract: Choosing the right hospital for surgery is an important decision for patients and their families. Whether it is a planned procedure or a surgery recommended after diagnosis, patients should carefully evaluate the hospital's surgical expertise, infrastructure, safety standards, and post-operative care. When searching for the best surgical hospital in Bangalore, it is important to look beyond reputation. A suitable hospital should have experienced specialists, well-equipped operation theatres, appropriate critical care facilities, and a team that supports patients throughout their treatment journey. Bangalore has several multi-speciality and dedicated surgical hospitals offering different treatment options. Understanding what to look for can help patients make informed healthcare decisions. What Makes a Good Surgical Hospital? A good surgical hospital combines medical expertise, appropriate infrastructure, patient safety, and coordinated care. The following factors can help patients evaluate their options. 1. Experienced Surgeons and Medical Specialists The expertise of the surgical team is one of the most important factors to consider. Patients should understand the proposed anaesthesia method, possible risks, pain management arrangements, and monitoring procedures. 5. Hygiene and Sterilisation Standards Infection prevention is an important part of surgical safety. Hospitals should follow proper cleaning, sterilisation, and infection-control practices. A Central Sterile Supply Department (CSSD) supports the cleaning, sterilisation, storage, and distribution of medical instruments used during procedures. 6. Post-Operative Care and Recovery Support Surgical care does not end when the procedure is completed. Patients may need monitoring, medication, wound care, rehabilitation, and follow-up consultations. Before selecting a hospital, ask how post-operative care is organised and who will guide you during recovery. 7. Transparent Costs and Insurance Assistance The total cost of surgery depends on several factors, including the procedure, surgeon's fees, anaesthesia, hospital stay, investigations, and medicines. Patients should request a written estimate and understand what is included. It is also useful to check insurance coverage, cashless treatment availability, and any additional expenses that may arise. title: Minimally invasive and nephron-sparing surgery for renal cancer: a nationwide analysis of 228,185 nephrectomies in Germany, 2011–2024
abstract: PURPOSE: Nephron-sparing and minimally invasive surgery are recommended for localised renal cell carcinoma, but the evidence comes from expert centres. We examined whether their advantages hold in routine care and whether access is equitable. METHODS: We analysed all 228,185 adult nephrectomies for renal cancer in the German hospital census, 2011-2024. Outcomes were in-hospital mortality, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE-RN), acute kidney injury, dialysis and length of stay. Access was compared by mixed-effects logistic regression with random hospital intercepts, procedure type by inverse probability of treatment weighting. RESULTS: The minimally invasive share rose from 19.7% to 59.4%, robot assistance from 9.7% to 79.4% of those, and partial nephrectomy overtook radical in 2017, reaching 62.5%. Adjusted odds were lower with minimally invasive access for death (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.42-0.56), MACCE-RN (0.56) and acute kidney injury (0.57), with a 21% shorter stay, and lower still with robot assistance than laparoscopy for acute kidney injury (0.46 vs. 0.72) and dialysis (0.67 vs. 0.92). Partial nephrectomy was associated with lower odds of death (0.61) and dialysis (0.41), without a shift towards patients with greater comorbidity. Minimally invasive surgery had ever been performed in 17.9% of the smallest and 95.9% of the largest centres. CONCLUSION: Both approaches became predominant and in routine care were associated with the advantages reported from expert centres. These are observational associations, not evidence of intrinsic superiority: administrative data carry no tumour stage and no follow-up beyond discharge. Adoption depended on hospital volume, not patient characteristics.

title: Automated EEG seizure detection in neonates with hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy using temporal and morphological modeling
abstract: Background Seizures are common in neonates with hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and may be difficult to recognize clinically. Automated electroencephalography (EEG) analysis is therefore important for neonatal neurological monitoring. However, variable EEG backgrounds, brief abnormal discharges, and marked inter-patient differences remain major challenges. Methods We developed a temporal EEG framework for neonatal seizure detection. Multi-scale temporal convolution was used to capture local waveform changes, while a hierarchical state-space encoder modeled longer temporal dependencies. Micro-temporal morphological evolution gating, temporal-state attention pooling, and nuisance-state suppression were further introduced to enhance seizure-related information. The model was evaluated on the Helsinki dataset of 79 neonates and an independent clinical HIE cohort of 34 neonates. EEG signals were converted to an 18-channel longitudinal bipolar montage and segmented into 10 s windows with a 5 s stride. Patient-level stratified five-fold cross-validation was performed under the SPEED evaluation framework. Results On the Helsinki dataset, the model achieved an AUC of 94.78 % ± 2.75 %, AP of 82.58 % ± 11.46 %, F1 score of 75.69 % ± 11.81 %, and MCC of 73.48 % ± 11.37 %. Sensitivity and Specificity were 70.42 % ± 13.59 % and 98.16 % ± 1.15 %, respectively. On the clinical cohort, the corresponding values were 95.51 % ± 2.36 %, 84.24 % ± 10.31 %, 77.31 % ± 10.48 %, and 75.29 % ± 10.08 %, with Sensitivity of 71.28 % ± 12.14 % and Specificity of 98.54 % ± 0.63 %. Ablation and patient-level analyses supported the complementary contributions of morphology modeling, temporal-state selection, and interference suppression. Conclusion The proposed framework achieved consistent seizure detection performance in both public and clinical neonatal HIE EEG datasets. It may provide useful technical support for automated seizure screening and bedside neurological monitoring in neonates with HIE.

title: Multidimensional frailty profiles and six-month all-cause readmission in hospitalized older patients with heart failure: a latent profile analysis
abstract: Background The early post-discharge period is the highest-risk window for older patients with heart failure, yet risk assessment remains centered on cardiac indicators. Frailty spans physical, nutritional, cognitive, psychological, and social domains, but most studies used a summary score or a frail vs. non-frail dichotomy, which cannot separate individuals with similar scores but distinct affected domains. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort included 423 patients aged 65 years or older hospitalized for heart failure from January 2022 to June 2025 who completed a structured predischarge frailty assessment. Latent profile analysis used eight standardized indicators across five domains. The primary endpoint was all-cause readmission within 6 months (180 days), assessed with Kaplan–Meier and Cox models. Competing risk, three-step, and missing-data sensitivity analyses were performed. Additional models further adjusted for the Fried phenotype score. Results The Bayesian and consistent Akaike information criteria were minimal at four profiles: relatively robust (C1, 26.2%), psychosocial frailty (C2, 18.0%), physical-nutritional frailty (C3, 35.5%), and multidomain severe frailty (C4, 20.3%), with almost opposite affected domains in C2 and C3. Readmission occurred in 122 patients (28.8%), and 6-month cumulative rates rose from 18.3% (C1) to 51.2% (C4) (log-rank P < 0.001). Fully adjusted hazard ratios vs. C1 were 2.90 (95% CI, 1.61 to 5.23) for C4, 1.64 (0.95 to 2.85) for C3, and 1.20 (0.59 to 2.41) for C2. Findings persisted with death as a competing event. After further adjustment for the Fried score, the association was attenuated (C4 hazard ratio 1.53, 0.67 to 3.49), and profile membership did not improve prediction beyond the Fried score. Conclusions Multidimensional frailty resolved into four profiles of differing configuration. Global involvement was associated with a higher 6-month readmission risk, whereas psychosocial impairment showed no independent association. This gradient largely reflected overall frailty burden. The profiles mainly describe which domains are affected, and their use in transitional care requires external validation.

title: Diagnostics in constraint : integrating evidence to advance patient-centred infectious disease diagnostics in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Infectious diseases remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries despite advances in prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed numerous challenges in healthcare systems and renewed efforts to strengthen diagnostic research, development, and implementation capacity across Sub-Saharan Africa. Central nervous system (CNS) infections exemplify these challenges, as diagnosis in many low-resource settings still relies on slow, less sensitive conventional microbiological methods. Rapid multiplex molecular tests, such as the FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel, may improve pathogen detection in CNS infections, but evidence on their implementation and utility in low-resource contexts remains limited. Moreover, high mortality and neurological sequelae persist despite pathogen identification, highlighting the need for prognostic biomarkers to support risk stratification and clinical management. Beyond technical innovation, developing responsive diagnostics research ecosystems relies on public participation and the use of biological samples, yet evidence on patient and public perspectives on biomedical research and biobanking remains limited across many African contexts. This project aimed to generate context-specific evidence to advance patient-centred infectious disease diagnostics and prognostic approaches, while informing the development of a sustainable and participatory diagnostics research ecosystem in sub-Saharan African settings. The studies spanned two clinical trials: the PI-POC trial, where clinical utility (Study I), disease burden (Study II), and protein profiling (Study III) studies were carried out; and the HOLICARE trial, where patient perspectives on biobanking as infrastructure for research and diagnostics development were explored across Uganda, Senegal and Ethiopia (Study IV). The multiplex molecular diagnostic (FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel) (Study I) reduced clinical turnaround time from the conventional 2 days for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture to 4.2 hours, with 75% of that time attributable to sample transport before analysis and reporting results to clinicians. The molecular diagnostic also significantly improved bacterial yield in CSF and enabled viral detection; however, with diagnostic uncertainty for HHV-6 detection. Hospitalisation length was significantly reduced for patients with negative results from the molecular diagnostic used for clinical decision-making. Mortality rates and antimicrobial administration did not differ significantly between the index and reference groups. Mortality in suspected CNS infections remains high (15%), with another 18% being discharged with neurological sequelae (Study II). S. pneumoniae was the most common bacterial pathogen detected, and HHV-6 the most common viral pathogen detected. Blood culture also detected several pathogens not included in the FA-ME panel, including Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus. Delayed capillary refill (adjusted risk ratio [ARR] 5.9; 95% Cl 1.8-20.0), symptomatic anaemia (aRR 2.7; 95% CI 1.1-7.0) and increased peripheral white blood cell count (aRR 3.3; 95% CI 1.8-6.1) were associated with increased risk of in-hospital mortality. Protein profiling of plasma samples from CNS infection patients (Study III) showed that 39/41 proteins in the panel were significantly more abundant in patients with fatal outcomes than in those who survived; however, heterogeneity was observed among fatal cases. Significantly abundant proteins were associated with neuroglial injury, vascular/endothelial disturbance, innate immunity, the acute-phase response, and metabolic stress. Glial fibrillary acidic protein showed moderate capability to discriminate fatal from non-fatal outcomes and warrants further validation. The survey on patient perspectives on biobanking (Study IV) showed that prior awareness of biobanking was low across the three countries, despite high willingness to participate. A generally positive attitude toward aspects of biobanking, such as trust in researchers, was associated with willingness to participate. Ugandan patients had higher odds of willingness to participate in biobanking than Ethiopian patients. Differences in preferences for biobanking consent were not marked, although broad consent was the most preferred model. Together, these findings demonstrate that diagnostic effectiveness is context-dependent, reflecting not only technical performance but also the clinical, health system, and societal environments for which the diagnostics are developed and deployed. Rather than viewing diagnostics as standalone technologies, this thesis supports a broader perspective in which their effectiveness depends on the interaction between diagnostic performance, clinical decision-making, health system capacities, and public trust. title: Posicionamento da ABRAMEDE sobre superlotação e boarding no Departamento de Emergência
journal: JBMEDE - Jornal Brasileiro de Medicina de Emergência
abstract: Contexto. A superlotação dos Departamentos de Emergência (DE) é hoje um dos principais desafios da assistência em urgência no Brasil e no mundo. Longe de ser uma falha operacional isolada, expressa um desequilíbrio sistêmico entre demanda, capacidade assistencial e fluxo hospitalar, com repercussões sobre a segurança dos pacientes, a qualidade do cuidado e a saúde das equipes. Objetivo. Estabelecer definições técnicas, sintetizar as melhores evidências disponíveis e propor princípios orientadores para o enfrentamento da superlotação e do boarding nos DE brasileiros. Métodos. Um grupo de trabalho da Comissão de Diretrizes Clínicas da ABRAMEDE, composto por especialistas em superlotação, boarding e gestão hospitalar, revisou a literatura sobre determinantes, impactos e métricas de superlotação e formulou, por consenso, definições, indicadores, metas e recomendações adaptadas à realidade brasileira. Não foi realizada revisão sistemática; as declarações são de boas práticas. Resultados. O documento padroniza a terminologia, definindo superlotação como taxa de ocupação maior ou igual a 1, calculada sobre os espaços de cuidado formalmente destinados à assistência, sem contabilizar espaços improvisados, e boarding como o intervalo entre a decisão médica de internação e a saída física do paciente do DE. Sintetiza as evidências de impacto sobre mortalidade hospitalar, erros de medicação, atrasos em intervenções tempo-dependentes, tempo de permanência, custos, satisfação, burnout e violência contra profissionais. Discute os determinantes do fenômeno pela Lei de Little e pelo modelo de Asplin, destacando o paradoxo gerencial entre a maior governabilidade do gestor da emergência sobre a Passagem e o predomínio da Saída como mecanismo de superlotação no contexto brasileiro, no qual cerca de 45% dos pacientes presentes nos DE estão em boarding. Propõe um conjunto mínimo de métricas com metas, incluindo tempo de decisão médica menor que 6 horas, tempo de permanência menor que 6,5 horas nos pacientes não internados e menor que 24 horas nos internados, e tempo de boarding menor que 12 horas. Apresenta ainda princípios e estratégias operacionais, entre elas política de gestão de altas, nivelamento da programação cirúrgica eletiva e das altas, salas de alta, huddles operacionais, monitoramento em tempo real da capacidade e planos de contingência, além de recomendações a gestores públicos e formuladores de políticas. Conclusão. A superlotação não é inevitável nem exclusiva da Emergência. Enquanto for tratada como um problema do DE, e não como manifestação de disfunção do fluxo hospitalar, a solução permanecerá fora de alcance.

title: Impact of subspecialty renaming on operational performance in a tertiary oncology hospital: a 24-month interrupted time-series analysis of the head and neck to head, neck, and thyroid surgery transition
abstract: Department renaming to reflect subspecialty focus is increasingly used to clarify clinical scope for patients and referrers, but evidence on its operational impact is scarce. This study evaluated the effect of renaming the Head and Neck Surgery Department as the Head, Neck, and Thyroid Surgery Department at a tertiary oncology hospital in China on operational performance and on thyroid-specific surgical volume and case mix. This single-center interrupted time-series study compared 12 pre-renaming months (January–December 2024) with 12 post-renaming months (February 2025–January 2026). We analyzed 42 operational indicators across six domains and 10 thyroid-specific indicators (procedure type, radiofrequency ablation, pathological category, and stage) using pre–post comparisons, trend and segmented regression, exploratory correlations, chi-square tests, and structural decomposition of total billed charges. After renaming, monthly discharges increased by 14.3% ( p = 0.084), DRG total weight by 19.9% ( p = 0.024), and surgical caseload by 21.4% ( p = 0.021); 82% of the growth in total billed charges reflected volume, not per-case charges. The Case Mix Index (1.45 vs. 1.53) and quality indicators did not deteriorate. Operated thyroid malignancies increased from 998 to 1,224 (+ 22.6%; p = 0.043) and central compartment neck dissections from 956 to 1,198 (+ 25.3%; p = 0.031), with an unchanged stage distribution (stage I: 95.0% vs. 94.0%; p = 0.397); thyroid cases accounted for 59.0% of additional procedures. However, the thyroid share of surgical procedures was stable (65.1% vs. 64.0%; p = 0.448), radiofrequency ablation remained rare (8 vs. 1), and segmented regression detected no abrupt change at the renaming date. The lower Level IV surgery proportion (61.8% vs. 45.8%) is suspected to result from a January 2025 revision of the surgical grading directory. Growth occurred despite the departure of two thyroid-focused surgeons. Subspecialty renaming was associated with volume growth without deterioration in case complexity or quality. Most additional thyroid cases were stage I cancers, but thyroid and non-thyroid surgery grew in parallel, indicating proportionate expansion of a thyroid-dominant service rather than a selective shift in case mix. Explicit subspecialty naming may help patients identify the appropriate service, although causal attribution requires controlled studies.
