Trained to engineer, hired to repair: jurisdictional subordination and the ceiling on health technology capability in Ghana
abstract: Ghana has taught biomedical engineering for more than two decades, yet within nine months the state described the profession as both absent from its hospitals and technically weak within them. The two statements are not strictly contradictory, but responses they invite miss what is actually wrong. The binding constraint is neither the number of graduates nor the quality of their training, but the narrowness of the task domain assigned to the profession. Three mechanisms hold that domain in place. The World Health Organization's Global Health Observatory carries separate series for biomedical engineers and biomedical technicians, but its only published definition merges the two, no definition of biomedical technician exists, and every series has stood unchanged since 2017; Ghana's return of 450 engineers against 39 technicians is irreconcilable with its payroll figures and observed hiring. The assigned jurisdiction, equipment maintenance, is work biomedical equipment technicians perform competently and more cheaply, so engineers are displaced from below while the design jurisdiction above goes unclaimed. And domestic demand for the wider work is limited and institutionally unstructured rather than absent. Set against the five domains in which Ghanaian biomedical engineers are trained, routine practice engages the service end if a single domain. The remedy is demand-side and definitional before it is institutional: separate the workforce count, define an establishment and a scope of practice, and apply the margin of preference already in Ghana's procurement law to a defined device schedule. A dedicated institution, if warranted, belongs last and should be developmental rather than regulatory.

title: Urban heat islands, climate change, and evolving disease landscapes in India: A public health review
journal: Journal of Preventive Medicine and Holistic Health
abstract: The convergence of the Urban Heat Island (UHI) phenomenon, accelerating climate change, and unchecked urban expansion has produced a public health emergency of unprecedented scale across India. Localized microclimatic warming is reshaping the epidemiology of both infectious and chronic disease, altering the transmission dynamics of vector-borne, re-emerging, and neglected tropical illnesses. Exposure to UHI conditions worsens classic heat-related illness, precipitates acute cardiovascular events, accelerates chronic kidney decline through recurrent dehydration, and triggers severe respiratory exacerbations. These health burdens fall unevenly across the population, reflecting historical patterns of urban design that stretch from colonial-era town planning to post-independence industrial growth. This review examines how rising temperatures amplifying with the UHI effect drive distinct health burdens in India and abroad, traces the historical roots of urban planning-linked social health inequities, and proposes strategies to cool Indian cities. Effective mitigation demands a shift from reactive disaster response to proactive, equity-centred urban planning that embeds microclimate adaptation within primary healthcare delivery and scales up municipal Heat Action Plans.

title: Echocardiography Pathway Improvement to Increase Capacity (EPIIC): A National Scoping Survey of Scientist-Led Echocardiography Clinics in the UK
abstract: Background Increasing demand for echocardiography in the United Kingdom (UK), alongside persistent workforce shortages, contribute to diagnostic delays. Scientist-led echocardiography clinics integrating imaging and clinical assessment in a single visit, may improve service efficiency and patient experience. However, the national extent of adoption is poorly characterised, and standardised guidance, competency frameworks and accreditation pathways are lacking. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey, the Echocardiography Pathway Improvement to Increase Capacity (EPIIC), was distributed electronically via British Society of Echocardiography (BSE) communication channels between 1 October 2025 and 15 January 2026. The survey evaluated six domains: demographics, service provision, clinic processes, perceived benefits and challenges, patient feedback and outcomes, and requirements for establishing scientist-led echocardiography clinics. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively to characterise current practice, while free-text responses underwent thematic categorisation. Results A total of 194 respondents completed the survey. Most identified as cardiac physiologists (67%) or clinical scientists (25%), with responses from all UK regions. An established scientist-led clinic was reported by 63% of respondents, with a further 13% reporting a service in pilot phase. Valve disease (81%) and heart failure (20%) were the most common indications. Clinics most frequently saw 0–10 patients per week (48%), with 60-minute appointments (56%). Internal cardiology referrals accounted for 89%. Echocardiography was included in 88% of protocols. Consultant cardiologist support was available in 72%, and structured escalation pathways were reported in 48%. Perceived benefits were strongly endorsed (> 80% agreement) across domains including patient access, waiting times, efficiency, patient experience and staff retention. Key challenges included funding (56%), staffing shortages (51%), accreditation gaps (34%), and limited consultant support (33%). Only 43% of respondents reported routinely collected formal or informal patient feedback, although free-text responses indicate largely positive feedback. Conclusion Scientist-led echocardiography clinics were reported across UK regions and healthcare settings but have developed with substantial variation in governance, competency standards, accreditation and outcome measurement. National and cross-specialty standardisation of scientist-led echocardiography clinics is required, with a purposeful prospective evaluation to determine whether actual clinical, patient and workforce benefits can be delivered consistently and sustainably.

title: Pace Layering the LongevityTech City
abstract: This chapter examines the application of Stewart Brand's Pace Layers framework to envision and design LongevityTech Cities, urban systems intentionally structured to support healthy, fulfilling, and inclusive living across extended lifespans by leveraging emerging technologies. Building on literature from longevity, urban planning, and design, this study uses three projects from MIT's Global Aging & The Built Environment course to address the unique temporal and systemic challenges of a longevity society. The adapted Pace Layers framework introduces two additional layers—Longevity and Technology—and plots them on temporal and spatial axes to examine the interactions between rapidly evolving innovations and more slowly changing infrastructures, governance, and culture. Three verbs—Inform, Influence, and Inspire—serve as relational links to illustrate how longevity, the needs of shifting demographics, inform technology, how technological interventions influence cities, and how cities, in turn, inspire new behaviors and perceptions surrounding the elderly. The discussion uses three student projects to demonstrate practical applications of LongevityTech Cities, ranging from hearing aid adoption services to the redesign of heart-failure patient discharge and age-ready community planning. By integrating academic theory with real-world design experimentation, this article presents an integrated yet flexible framework that aligns diverse stakeholders, balances innovation and stability, and fosters constructive turbulence to drive urban transformation in support of the well-being of multigenerational communities.

title: Evaluating the effectiveness of a digital therapy intervention (iCARE) to treat symptoms of postpartum depression: study protocol for a two—armed randomized controlled trial
abstract: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common condition that can negatively affect maternal well-being and child development. Cognitive behavioral therapy an effective psychological treatment, but access is limited in many settings. Internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy offers a scalable alternative that can be delivered flexibly at home. This trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a self-guided internet-based intervention, iCARE, compared to treatment as usual for mothers with symptoms of PPD. This is a two-arm, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial. Mothers within 6 months postpartum with an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score of 7–30 will be recruited through health nurses in 21 Danish municipalities and nationwide via self-recruitment through a project website. After baseline assessment, participants will be randomized 1:1 to iCARE plus usual care or usual care alone, stratified by symptom severity and recruitment pathway. The primary outcome is change in depressive symptoms from baseline to two months, with a secondary endpoint at 6 months. Key secondary outcomes include anxiety, functioning, automatic negative thoughts, and parental stress. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Missing data will be handled with multiple imputation. Safety procedures include monitoring of symptom scores and predefined referral pathways for participants reporting self-harm thoughts or deterioration of depressive symptoms. This trial will provide evidence on the effectiveness and safety of a self-guided digital intervention for PPD in a real-world setting. If effective, iCARE could improve access to psychological support and reduce treatment gaps for mothers experiencing symptoms of PPD and potentially be implemented in a stepped care approach. Findings will inform future implementation strategies in public health systems. ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT07384273

title: Understanding pregnancy outcome classification from community to routine health information systems in a north Indian district using a mixed-methods approach: insights from the SHRiSTI implementation research
abstract: Background Accurate classification of pregnancy outcomes is essential for maternal and child health surveillance, health system planning, and evidence-based policy formulation. However, potential misclassification of pregnancy outcomes remains an understudied issue, particularly in the Indian context where pregnancy outcome reporting is shaped by interactions across community and facility levels. This study explores these discrepancies within a context of high institutional delivery coverage and active maternal and child health surveillance and investigates how pregnancy outcomes are interpreted, classified, and documented across community and health system interfaces in a district in North India. Methods This study employed an explanatory sequential mixed method design within the broader Strategies to Help in Optimal Pregnancy Outcomes and Reduce Stillbirths in India (SHRiSTI) implementation research study. Quantitative data were collected through a community health survey of 3,000 women with a recorded birth outcome. While qualitative data were generated through in-depth interviews with seven women who had experienced adverse birth outcomes, key informant interview with seven health care personnel (three Medical Officers, two Auxiliary Nurse Midwifes, and two Information Assistants) and two focus group discussion with Accredited Social Health Activist (n = 11). The data for this study were collected between the formative and scale up phases of the SHRiSTI, an ongoing implementation study in a district in Haryana, India. Results Differences in pregnancy-outcome classification were identified across the community survey, ASHA surveillance records, and HMIS. Qualitative findings demonstrated that misclassification operates through multiple intersecting processes across different levels of reporting. Within community, vernacular terminology and locally embedded understandings shaped how pregnancy losses were described and communicated by women and their family members. Among frontline health workers, definitional uncertainty regarding abortion and stillbirth categories influenced reporting practices, while at the facility level, institutional documentation procedures and recording practices further contributed to inconsistencies in classification and reporting. Conclusion Potential misclassification of pregnancy outcomes reflects both system-level limitations and socio-cultural processes embedded within reproductive health reporting practices. The study recommends that targeted training of frontline health workers, standardization of pregnancy outcome definitions, and strengthened community-to-facility data linkages may improve the accuracy of both surveillance systems and data quality.

title: Integrated Group Antenatal Care Model: Development of a Brazilian Group Antenatal Care Programme Using Plan–Do–Study–Act Cycles
abstract: Background Group antenatal care (ANC-G) has emerged as an innovative model to improve the quality of antenatal care (ANC) by integrating clinical assessment, health education and psychosocial support. Although evidence supporting its effectiveness is growing, its implementation within public health systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains limited. Objective To describe the development, implementation and structure of an ANC-G programme. Methods This quality improvement report, prepared in accordance with the SQUIRE 2.0 guidelines, describes a programme implemented in a teaching hospital in Brazil. The programme was developed through iterative Plan–Do–Study–Act (PDSA) cycles during a pilot randomised study; the comparative outcomes of that study are not reported in this manuscript. Group sessions were scheduled according to participants’ gestational age, with one session in the postpartum period and 10 at the recommended timing for routine antenatal/postpartum care. All sessions were delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Results The programme comprised 11 structured group sessions, each lasting approximately 2 hours, involving 8–12 pregnant women, and facilitated by obstetric nurses, with participation from obstetricians, psychologists, a physical educator, nursing students, obstetrics resident and invited professionals, including nutritionists, physiotherapists and social workers. The model integrated all clinical/obstetric assessment with group-based health education, physical activity and psychosocial support. Topics addressed throughout the programme included nutrition, immunisation, physical activity, warning signs, infection prevention, mental health, gender-based violence, reproductive planning, birth preparedness, breastfeeding, newborn care, women’s rights and postpartum adaptation. The sessions incorporated participatory educational strategies, including group discussions, simulations, practical demonstrations, games, artistic activities, reflective writing and peer learning. The PDSA process enabled the development of a structured, contextually adapted programme and generated detailed documentation of programme content, implementation procedures, educational strategies and professional roles. Conclusions This study provides a comprehensive description of a structured ANC-G programme implemented in a university hospital. The programme offers a replicable framework for integrating clinical, educational, and psychosocial components of ANC and may inform future implementation and scale-up within public health systems. Trial registration: Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC), RBR-8xcjmf; UTN U1111-1243-6241. Registered on 26 February 2020.

title: Editorial: Dissemination and implementation science in medicine
abstract: Reply: Thank you for this feedback. We have added text to the introduction highlighting the breadth of implementation science applications in the collection, as well as common themes across articles.I suggest reviewing the article summaries to ensure a consistent distinction between feasibility, acceptability, adoption, fidelity, sustainability, and clinical or service outcomes. This is particularly relevant to the pilot and observational studies described. Where an initiative is characterized as successful or as improving care, the summary should briefly specify which outcome supports that statement and use language appropriate to the study design. Demonstrating feasibility, for example, does not in itself establish clinical effectiveness.Reply: We appreciate this feedback and have distinguished the implementation and effectiveness outcomes throughout the article summaries to clarify implementation success vs clinical/service impact.The collection includes studies addressing core components, modifications to implementation strategies, and service adaptation. These provide an opportunity to discuss a central implementation question: how to respond to local needs while preserving an intervention's essential components or functions. A short discussion of this relationship would strengthen the editorial's conceptual coherence. Where relevant, it would also help to distinguish adaptations to the intervention itself from adaptations to the strategies used to implement it.Reply: We agree that these questions are central to implementation science and have added text to the introduction highlighting this.The introduction and closing paragraph emphasize incorporating implementation science into medical education. However, this proposal receives relatively little attention in the main text. I recommend identifying a few competencies that follow from the work presented, such as recognizing contextual barriers, selecting appropriate implementation strategies, distinguishing clinical outcomes from implementation outcomes, and assessing fidelity and adaptation. The authors could also indicate where these competencies might fit within professional education and training. The statement that there is no established standard for incorporating implementation science into medical education would benefit from a supporting reference or a more clearly defined scope.Reply: We appreciate this feedback and have expanded the text related to health professions education to clarify its importance in the context of the larger article.The categories combine study designs, purposes, and types of contribution. This may be a reasonable way to organize an editorial, but the rationale should be explained briefly. In particular, I suggest checking the heading "Systematic Reviews," which includes an analysis of research grants and other papers whose status as systematic reviews is not clear from the descriptions. A broader heading might better reflect the work included.Reply: We agree with this feedback and have updated the section titles to the following: Guidance, Methods, and Tools; Qualitative Research; Descriptive and Observational Research; Quantitative and Mixed Methods Research; Review Articles; and Perspectives and Opinion.Before the invitation for new submissions, the editorial would benefit from a concluding paragraph identifying the collection's main contributions and two or three priorities for future work. A brief discussion of the conditions that may affect the transfer of these approaches between health systems would also be valuable. Resources, service organization, and local capacity are relevant considerations. Addressing these would help readers assess the applicability of the findings beyond the settings in which the studies were conducted.Reply: We appreciate this feedback and have added a concluding paragraph prior to the invitation for new submissions.Dissemination and Implementation science (D&I) is a field that focuses on understanding the best ways to translate evidence-based interventions, programs, and guidelines into practice. It aims to bridge the gap between research and practice by systematically studying the methods and strategies that promote the adoption, implementation, and sustainability of evidence-based interventions in real-world settings. Implementation science provides models and frameworks to guide the design, evaluation, and dissemination of effective implementation strategies that can improve the delivery of health care services and the health outcomes of individuals and populations. It also helps identify barriers and facilitators to the implementation process and guides solutions to overcome those barriers. The field has wide-ranging applications across various fields, including medicine and health care, public health, education, and social services.There is currently no set standard of incorporating implementation science into accredited health professions education curricula or subsequent training, an area where its inclusion could be especially advantageous. As the field of implementation science grows and advances, it is increasingly important for healthcare practitioners to understand the field's guiding principles and varied applications. Essential implementation science competencies for healthcare practitioners include identifying important contextual factors (barriers and facilitators), selecting and evaluating implementation strategies, defining and distinguishing clinical and implementation outcomes, and assessing fidelity and adaptation. These tenets of implementation science will help healthcare professionals develop the knowledge and skills necessary to critically evaluate research and translate it into clinical practice.The inaugural research topic Dissemination and Implementation Science in Medicine includes 31 articles that reflect the evolving field of implementation science and demonstrate the broad application of evidence-based interventions, practices, and policies across real-world settings that help move the implementation science field forward. The articles included in this research topic are categorized below into Guidance, Methods, and Tools, Qualitative Research, Descriptive and Observational Research; Quantitative and Mixed Methods Research, Review Articles, and Perspectives and Opinion. These categories illuminate the expanding scope and breadth of D&I across health care ressearch and the use of innovative methodologies and increased adherence to D&I frameworks and models to expand the D&I knowledge base. The final two sections, Review Articles and Perspectives and Opinion provide guidance on future directions.As a whole, this collection demonstrates the breadth of the application of implementation science methods as well as common themes across these applications. Themes across articles include the importance of leadership support, interprofessional collaboration and partnerships, collaborative learning, and contextual adaptation for implementation success. The field of implementation science, which evaluates interventions and implementation strategies in complex real-world contexts, continues to have robust ongoing discussions about issues and questions inherent to these complex and varied settings. As demonstrated in this collection, researchers must consider questions such as how to balance fidelity (maintaining the core components of an intervention or implementation strategy) with contextual adaptation, and determine and clearly define their approaches to these questions, with different approaches appropriate to different interventions and contexts. On a final note, many of us remember our dear friend and colleague, Dr. Bryan Garner. Dr. Sara Becker along with other colleagues and friends kindly provide a published contributions to the field of implementation science commemorative article remembering Bryan's significant impact in the field.31. Becker, et al. reflect on Dr. Bryan R. Garner's contributions to the field of implementation science. They outline his expansive work in addressing sta^ turnover, implementation climate, multi-level implementation strategies, novel study designs, and pragmatic tools and measures.This inaugural Dissemination and Implementation Science in Medicine collection highlights the broad and varied applications of implementation science methods, as well as unifying themes and common challenges. As demonstrated in this collection, the field of implementation science continues to hone and apply methods that grapple with the complexities of translating and implementing interventions across diverse settings with varying resources, capacity, and other contextual factors. These questions and considerations will remain central as the field continues to move forward.We have opened Volume II of the Dissemination and Implementation Science in Medicine topic area, now positioned in the new Experimental, Translational, and Evidence-Based Medicine in Frontiers in Medicine journal, which focuses on translating medical research and innovation into improved patient care.

title: Peripheral norepinephrine in perioperative and critical care medicine: a narrative review of evidence, safety boundaries, and clinical governance
abstract: Peripheral administration of norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is increasingly used for vasodilatory hypotension in the operating room, post-anesthesia care unit, emergency department and intensive care unit. Contemporary guidance now permits short-term peripheral administration under defined conditions, but the supporting thresholds are largely consensus-based and vary across settings. This narrative review synthesizes recent perioperative and critical care evidence, vascular-access standards, extravasation management literature, adverse-event reporting concepts and an illustrative perioperative extravasation case. Available data suggest that severe tissue injury is rare with short peripheral catheters, whereas minor adverse-event and extravasation rates depend strongly on definitions, surveillance intensity, device type and case selection. We therefore focus not on whether peripheral norepinephrine is simply “safe,” but on how to govern it as a monitored bridge: patient and access selection, explicit dose-duration boundaries, documented site surveillance, timely escalation, extravasation rescue, and measurable outcomes including protocol adherence, threshold exceedance, CVC avoidance and injury severity.

title: The cost of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Australia: estimates from linked state-based health data
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of acute hospitalisations in Australia, yet its true health system cost is poorly defined. We estimated the direct healthcare costs attributable to COPD using linked primary and secondary care data. METHODS: A cross-sectional analysis of linked general practice, hospital, emergency department and mortality records from Western Australia was conducted. Individuals with COPD who were alive in 2021 were identified from primary care diagnoses, hospital records (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Australian Modification J44) or spirometry recording. Each COPD case was matched to one individual without COPD on age, sex, smoking status and history of atherosclerosis. Direct healthcare costs were calculated from a government payer perspective, including hospitalisations, emergency presentations, general practice services, prescribed medicines, ambulance transport and pathology testing. RESULTS: The cohort included 6811 patients with COPD (median age 69 years; 51% female) and 6811 matched controls. Individuals with COPD had A$6584 higher adjusted annual healthcare costs than matched controls, with excess costs driven largely by hospitalisations. Hospitalisations accounted for 68% of attributable costs, followed by emergency presentations (17%) and medications (7%). Nationally, COPD accounted for an estimated A$3.87 billion in direct healthcare costs in 2021. CONCLUSIONS: COPD imposes a substantial and preventable health system burden, dominated by hospitalisations for acute exacerbations and comorbid conditions. Improved recognition, maintenance therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation and ambulatory care models may help reduce avoidable admissions and associated costs.

title: PROVISION OF PHYSICAL ACTIVITY IN PRIMARY HEALTH CARE SERVICES: A SCOPING REVIEW WITH META-AGGREGATION
authors: Julian Lennon Gonçalves de Souza Leite
abstract: A promoção da atividade física (AF) na Atenção Primária à Saúde (APS) é essencial para prevenir e controlar doenças crônicas não transmissíveis. Contudo, sua implementação ainda enfrenta barreiras estruturais, desigualdades regionais e insuficiente capacitação profissional. Este estudo mapeou evidências sobre a promoção da AF na APS, identificando fragilidades e potencialidades. Realizou-se uma revisão de escopo conforme PRISMA-ScR nas bases Web of Science, Scopus, LILACS, MEDLINE e Catálogo CAPES. Após triagem, 20 estudos foram incluídos. Os artigos revisados por pares (n = 15) foram analisados no IRaMuTeQ. Os termos mais frequentes foram “Atividade física”, “Usuário”, “APS” e “Aconselhamento”. A análise de similitude identificou a AF como núcleo conceitual, relacionada a fatores individuais, institucionais e metodológicos. Emergiram seis classes temáticas: oferta de AF na APS; competência profissional; instrumentos de avaliação; desigualdade regional; estratégias de implementação; e infraestrutura/acesso. Os achados revelaram infraestrutura insuficiente, disparidades territoriais e lacunas na formação profissional, além de potencialidades como o Programa Academia da Saúde, aconselhamento e ações interdisciplinares. Em síntese, a promoção da AF na APS depende de investimentos em infraestrutura, qualificação profissional e estratégias adaptadas ao território para garantir equidade e sustentabilidade no SUS.

title: Maternal and newborn survival in Somalia: burden, inequities, health-system challenges, and the path toward universal health coverage
journal: Frontiers in Global Women s Health
abstract: Maternal and newborn mortality remains a major public health challenge in Somalia, where conflict, poverty, displacement, geographic inequity, and health-system fragility constrain access to effective care. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on the epidemiological burden, determinants, health-system performance, Universal Health Coverage (UHC), and strategic priorities for maternal and newborn survival. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched, with supplementary searches of the WHO Global Health Library, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and repositories of WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, the World Bank, UN IGME, MMEIG, and Somali health authorities. The core search covered January 2000 to April 2026. Of approximately 212 records identified, 98 full-text sources were assessed and 61 were included in the final narrative synthesis. Population-level estimates indicate a maternal mortality ratio of 621 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020 (95% uncertainty interval: 436–888) and a neonatal mortality rate of 35.1 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022. Evidence consistently identifies inadequate emergency obstetric and newborn care, workforce shortages, weak referral systems, limited primary healthcare capacity, high out-of-pocket spending, and socioeconomic and geographic inequities as major constraints. Recent national facility evidence improves understanding of service availability and readiness, but nationally representative data on effective EmONC coverage, quality of newborn care, and maternal and perinatal death surveillance remain limited. Accelerating survival gains requires stronger primary healthcare, emergency care, workforce and referral systems, strategic purchasing and regulation of non-state providers, financial protection, and equity-focused multisectoral action within the UHC framework. These findings indicate the need to redefine what constitutes progress in neonatal, and by extension maternal, care in LMICs, moving beyond aggregate coverage gains toward measures of effective access, quality, equity, continuity of care, and protection of populations that remain poorly served.

title: Drug Supply Chain Security Act applicability to emergency medical services medication replenishment programs: Implications for health-system pharmacy
Organizational structure and quality of pharmaceutical supply chain management in internally displaced person (IDP) camps in Ethiopia. A qualitative study
abstract: Pharmaceutical supply chain management (PSCM) in humanitarian setting is essential for ensuring the availability, quality, and safe distribution of medicines. However, managing pharmaceutical supplies in internally displaced persons (IDP) settings is challenging because of complex organizational arrangements, multiple stakeholders, and resource constraints. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the organizational structure, operational processes, and quality of PSCM in IDP camps in Ethiopia. A qualitative study was conducted using in-depth interviews with key stakeholders, including health professionals, cluster health center staff, and representatives from government and donor organizations. Interviews explored procurement, storage, distribution, inventory management, reporting, and supply chain coordination. Data were analyzed thematically to identify key themes and sub-themes reflecting the strengths and challenges of PSCM in IDP settings. Findings revealed a multi-level and coordinated supply chain system involving federal, regional, zonal, cluster, and IDP site levels, integrating both government and partner-supplied medicines. Key challenges included inadequate storage infrastructure, lack of cold chain systems, fragmented and manual inventory management, and weak logistics management information systems (LMIS). Frequent stock-outs and unreliable medicine availability were reported, driven by centralized procurement, donor dependence, and weak forecasting. Data inaccuracies and limited use of supply chain information for decision-making further constrained responsiveness. Concerns regarding medicine quality assurance were also highlighted, including exposure to adverse storage conditions, expired medicines, and diversion. Despite structured distribution and reporting mechanisms, gaps in coordination, supervision, and contingency planning hindered consistent service delivery. The PSCM system in IDP camps demonstrates structured coordination and integration of multiple stakeholders but is undermined by infrastructural limitations, weak information systems, and inconsistent governance. Strengthening storage and cold chain capacity, improving LMIS functionality, enhancing inventory management, and reinforcing supervision and accountability mechanisms are essential to ensure medicine availability, maintain quality, and support uninterrupted healthcare delivery for displaced populations. Not applicable.

title: Degradation-Aware Sizing and Dispatch of Photovoltaic and LFP Battery Storage for a Lahore Hospital under Load-Shedding
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Hospitals cannot defer electricity demand in the way other commercial buildings can: operating theatres, intensive care, cold-chain storage and life-safety systems must remain supplied through every grid outage. In Lahore, Pakistan, prolonged load-shedding makes that requirement a sizing and control problem rather than a simple backup-generator problem. This study sizes photovoltaic (PV) generation and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery storage for a hospital in Lahore under load-shedding, using an hourly simulation over 8,760 hours. Solar resource is taken from two independent sources — a Photovoltaic Geographical Information System (PVGIS) typical meteorological year (1,868 kWh/m²/year) and NASA POWER hourly data for the actual year 2025 (1,706 kWh/m²/year) — and demand is represented by a transparent, reproducible synthetic hospital load of 823.7 MWh/year (peak 191 kW), of which 525.1 MWh/year (63.7%) is critical load after a correction described in full. Sixteen PV–battery combinations (PV 100–300 kWp × LFP 100–400 kWh) are tested under three outage scenarios (4, 8 and 12 hours per day) and two dispatch rules, with PV degradation tested at the standard warranty rate of 0.5%/year and at a Punjab field rate of 1.63%/year. Bills are computed at the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) flat commercial tariff of Rs 39.76/kWh with exports credited at the 2026 net-billing rate of Rs 8.13/kWh. Without PV or storage, 177.2 MWh/year of critical load is unserved in the base case of 8 outage hours per day. The central finding is that dispatch matters more than battery size. If the battery is charged only from PV surplus (Dispatch A), daytime hospital load absorbs almost all PV output, the battery is usually empty when an outage begins, and 69.5–121.4 MWh/year of critical load remains unserved even at the largest sizes tested. If the battery is charged from the grid in the three hours before each scheduled outage block so that it is full when the outage starts (Dispatch B), unserved critical load falls to zero in the base case from 100 kWp PV with 200 kWh storage upward. The central case adopted in this paper is 300 kWp PV with 200 kWh LFP under Dispatch B: in the base case it generates 437.5 MWh/year, imports 388.4 MWh/year, exports 26.7 MWh/year, leaves unserved critical load at 0.00 MWh/year and bills Rs 15.22 million/year — Rs 5.92 million below the Rs 21.15 million no-system baseline — at about 775 equivalent full cycles per year. The smaller alternative, 200 kWp PV with 200 kWh LFP under the same dispatch, is the smallest system at the 200 kWp scale that reaches zero unserved critical load (annual bill Rs 18.37 million, a saving of Rs 2.78 million). Resilience under Dispatch B is bought with higher grid imports and much heavier battery cycling (about 550–1,160 equivalent full cycles per year, compared with about 2–350 under Dispatch A), which shortens cycling life to roughly 3–9 years against a 3,000–5,000-cycle LFP rating and must be priced into any procurement decision. The central case does not extend to severe outages: under severe 12-hour outages, 300 kWp with 200 kWh under Dispatch B still leaves 21.3 MWh/year of critical load unserved, and near-zero severe cover requires 200 kWp with 300 kWh under Dispatch B, which leaves only 0.06 MWh/year unserved. PV degradation at the field rate reduces output by 15.1% by Year 10, but Dispatch B still holds unserved critical load at zero because grid charging compensates; the degradation cost appears in the bill instead. Because self-consumption is 94–100% at the sizes tested, the low net-billing export price has little effect on these results. No payback period is claimed, because capital costs were not priced from quotations. The single most valuable next step is to replace the synthetic load with the hospital's measured SCADA log or twelve months of electricity bills and to re-run the identical model.

title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems
journal: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
abstract: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.

title: How Ready Are Aceh and West Sumatra to Implement Reproductive Health Services During Disasters?
journal: Journal of Public Health and Pharmacy
abstract: Introduction: Indonesia’s recurrent disasters can disrupt routine health services and threaten continuity of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) care. Pre-crisis readiness to activate the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP), adapted in Indonesia as the Paket Pelayanan Awal Minimum (PPAM), is therefore important in disaster-prone provinces such as Aceh and West Sumatra. This study compared readiness-related capacities for MISP/PPAM implementation in Aceh and West Sumatra and identified shared and province-specific policy, coordination, data, resources, and service-related gaps. Methods: A comparative province-level structured consensus assessment was conducted from October 2024 to January 2025. Sixteen purposively selected multisectoral stakeholders in each province (32 in total) participated in facilitated focus group discussions using an Indonesian adaptation of the 2020 MISP Readiness Assessment. The adapted instrument contained 73 items. Province-level responses, supporting evidence, focus group minutes, and action-planning outputs were consolidated into a domain-by-province matrix. Domain categories were retained as consensus-based categorical judgments and were not treated as interval-scale scores. A structured narrative synthesis was used to interpret the basis of each rating. Results: Both provinces received an “Adequate” rating for the policy, coordination, data, and resource domain and favorable “Good” ratings across most service-related domains. In Aceh, adolescent reproductive health and minimum health services for children under five were rated “Adequate”; the remaining service-related domains were rated “Good.” West Sumatra received “Good” ratings across all service-related domains. Important residual gaps included incomplete crisis-specific SRH governance, limited formal engagement of non-government actors, incomplete integration of PPAM/MISP indicators and sex-, age-, and disability-disaggregated data, access barriers for marginalized groups, and partially formalized referral pathways. Because many service-domain items assess routine service availability during stable periods, these favorable ratings represent readiness-related capacity rather than demonstrated emergency activation or service performance. Conclusion: Aceh and West Sumatra show favorable readiness-related capacity across most assessed service domains, but crisis-specific governance, coordination, data, referral, and inclusion gaps remain. The findings support targeted preparedness strengthening without implying that the assessment demonstrated real-time MISP activation, timeliness, quality, or equity during an actual emergency.

title: Preventable Healthcare Crisis: Why Do Millions of People With Dental Caries Require Emergency Care?
journal: Advances in Social Sciences Research Journal
abstract: Dental caries is the most common chronic disease of childhood and is largely preventable, yet children across the United States continue to experience severe dental pain, infections, abscesses, and complications requiring emergency department visits, hospitalization, and treatment under general anesthesia. The progression from an early carious lesion to a dental emergency rarely occurs without opportunities for prevention, early detection, and timely intervention. This article examines the systemic and socioeconomic factors that allow a manageable childhood disease to become a medical emergency, including the separation of oral health from general pediatric care, delayed preventive services, barriers to accessing dental treatment, limitations in Medicaid coverage, and inadequate continuity of care following emergency treatment. These challenges disproportionately affect children from low-income families, reinforcing persistent disparities in oral health outcomes. Although emergency departments play an essential role in managing acute complications, they cannot substitute for definitive dental treatment and sustained preventive care. Reducing avoidable dental emergencies requires a coordinated approach that integrates oral health into routine pediatric care, strengthens access to preventive and restorative services, addresses social determinants of health, and ensures timely follow-up. Ultimately, the true measure of progress in children's oral health should not be how effectively severe dental emergencies are managed, but how successfully health systems prevent children from reaching that point of suffering pain and losing their teeth and dental tissues.

title: LABORATORY REJECTION RATES, DETERMINANTS, DEPARTMENTAL VARIATIONS, AND HEALTHCARE IMPACT: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
abstract: **Project Overview** This systematic review and meta-analysis investigates clinical laboratory specimen rejection rates, underlying determinants, departmental variations, and downstream healthcare impacts across diverse healthcare settings. Pre-analytical errors account for approximately 60%–70% of all clinical laboratory errors and are heavily influenced by human, procedural, and organizational factors—such as test ordering, patient preparation, sample collection, labeling, transport, and storage—that often occur outside direct laboratory control. Because specimen rejection is a primary indicator of pre-analytical failure, synthesizing evidence across study settings and income contexts provides a comprehensive view of laboratory quality and patient safety. **Purpose and Objectives** The primary purpose of this study is to determine the overall prevalence/rate of laboratory sample rejection across clinical settings. Secondary objectives are to: * Identify key technical, administrative, and organizational determinants of specimen rejection (such as hemolysis, coagulation/clotting, insufficient sample volume, labeling or form errors, and transport/storage issues). * Examine variations in rejection rates across hospital departments and laboratory units (including emergency departments, inpatient wards, outpatient services, intensive care units, hematology, and clinical chemistry laboratories). * Evaluate the impact of specimen rejection across testing phases (pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical) and on clinical and operational outcomes, including turnaround time delays, repeat sampling/patient discomfort, financial costs, and diagnostic or therapeutic delays. * Assess differences in rejection rates and between-study heterogeneity across economic contexts (high-, middle-, and low-income settings) using random-effects proportional meta-analysis, subgroup analyses, sensitivity checks, and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) risk-of-bias appraisal. **Expected Outcomes** This project is expected to generate pooled prevalence estimates and variability metrics (such as 95% confidence intervals, Cochran's Q, and I² statistics) for specimen rejection rates overall and across key subgroups, alongside a structured synthesis of leading rejection causes, high-risk units, and patient/system impacts. In the underlying dataset of 38 included studies (spanning over 100 million total laboratory samples across multiple regions, with reported rejection rates ranging from 0.0004% to 9.31% and distinct pooled estimates across economic strata), the findings highlight how workflow complexity, resource constraints, and procedural standardization shape rejection risk. Ultimately, the review aims to support evidence-based quality improvement strategies—such as standardized phlebotomy and labelling protocols, targeted staff training, department-specific monitoring, and context-adapted quality indicators—to reduce specimen rejections, improve laboratory efficiency, and protect patient care.

title: Predisposing and prognostic factors of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing in patients with malignancies: a single-center retrospective study
abstract: Background: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is rising in patients with malignancies and is associated with higher morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to assess the diagnostic performance of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) for PJP and to identify risk factors for PJP occurrence and mortality in cancer patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Methods: We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 136 cancer patients with severe pneumonia admitted to the ICU of Jiangsu Cancer Hospital from September 2020 to September 2025. Pneumocystis jirovecii (P. jirovecii) and co-pathogens in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were detected via mNGS. Logistic regression analyses were performed to identify risk factors for PJP occurrence and 30-day mortality. Results: Of the 136 patients enrolled in this study, 25 were positive for PJP and 111 were negative for PJP based on BALF‑mNGS results. Mixed infections were more prevalent in PJP than non-PJP patients (P =0.024), particularly cytomegalovirus co‑infection (P =0.001). PJP occurrence was independently associated with radiotherapy (OR=3.867, 95% CI=1.274–11.737, P =0.017), immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy (OR=6.643, 95% CI=1.662–26.548, P =0.007), and malignant solid tumor (OR=0.107, 95% CI=0.019–0.611, P =0.012). Overall 30-day mortality was significantly higher in the PJP group than that in the non-PJP group (60.00% vs. 32.43%, P =0.013). In PJP patients, univariate analysis identified malignant solid tumor (OR=14.000, 95% CI=1.299–150.889, P =0.030), ICI therapy (OR=11.000, 95% CI=1.603–75.502, P =0.015), invasive mechanical ventilation (OR=6.000, 95% CI=1.003–35.908, P =0.050), and lower oxygenation index (OR=0.981, 95% CI=0.962–1.000, P =0.045) as mortality predictors, though none remained significant in multivariate analysis. Conclusions: Clinicians should maintain high suspicion for PJP in cancer patients with severe pneumonia, particularly those receiving radiotherapy and ICI therapy, as mNGS enables rapid and comprehensive detection of P. jirovecii and co-infecting pathogens.

title: A comparative study on living with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome: Was patient experience better in 2024 than in 2014?
abstract: Background Understanding patients’ experiences of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) is essential for better care and support. aHUS is an ultrarare, life-threatening disorder caused by uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, leading to endothelial damage, thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), acute kidney injury, and kidney failure. It requires specialist expertise for accurate diagnosis and effective management. Methods In 2014, the aHUS Alliance partnered with EURORDIS/RareConnect to poll the global aHUS community across five domains: diagnosis and genetics; treatment; information and support; societal impact; and access to centres of excellence, research and registries. In 2024, the Alliance repeated the poll to assess progress over the decade. Both used online questionnaires in English and several other languages to promote inclusivity. There were 217 respondents in 2014 and 296 in 2024. Responses were collated in Excel and compared using bar graphs. Results Respondents in 2024 were older and predominantly female. Diagnosis timelines decreased by 20%. While approximately 80% of patients underwent genetic testing in both surveys, results were obtained substantially faster in 2024 (47% within one month versus 17% in 2014). Access to effective treatment increased from 61% to 74%, driven by longer-acting complement inhibitors, whose use rose from 0% to 39% of patients. Sources of information and patient support were transformed. Awareness of societal impacts increased slightly, but just over half of respondents reported no additional burden. Coverage of expert centres (approximately 50%) and participation in research and registries (approximately 33%) showed little change. Conclusion Across surveys conducted ten years apart, meaningful progress in access to complement inhibitors was observed, with patients living longer and the condition predominantly affecting females. Significant challenges remain, particularly the need for more rapid diagnosis to optimise outcomes. Emerging communication technologies could further empower patients in daily life. Only half of respondents reported societal impacts, highlighting the need to better understand long-term effects on education and employment. Greater research participation and regular experience tracking are essential to improve quality of life for people living with aHUS.

title: Complicações e implicações sistêmicas associadas ao uso de medicamentos injetáveis para perda de peso
authors: Ana Paula Adry de O. Costa
abstract: This study analyzed adverse events and systemic implications associated with semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide used for weight loss. A qualitative narrative review summarized 15 core clinical publications, including randomized trials, secondary analyses, meta-analyses, and an observational study. Findings showed weight-loss efficacy and predominantly mild or moderate gastrointestinal events. A meta-analysis of 76 trials identified an increased relative risk of gallbladder and biliary diseases. Observational associations with pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, and gastroparesis require cautious causal interpretation. Cardiovascular benefit from semaglutide was demonstrated in patients with established cardiovascular disease, and weight regain followed withdrawal in specific studies. Lean mass loss alone does not establish sarcopenia. Individualized indications and monitoring should consider tolerability, hydration, body composition, and continuity of care. Non-systematic selection and heterogeneous publications limit the generalizability of the findings.

title: Prevenção de infecções em centro cirúrgico: abordagem multidisciplinar com POPs
abstract: The high-complexity perioperative environment requires the convergence of technical rigor in operational workflows and the continuous mitigation of healthcare risks. Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAIs) in the Surgical Center demands a systemic approach that overcomes fragmented practices, positioning the standardization of clinical conduct through regulatory guidelines and institutional protocols as an indispensable barrier to protect the surgical patient's integrity. This study aimed to analyze how hospital institutions can implement Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) grounded in process engineering and to outline the essential role of the multidisciplinary team in preventing Surgical Site Infections (SSIs) and strengthening the aseptic chain in the Surgical Center. An integrative literature review of a descriptive and qualitative nature was conducted. The documentary search was carried out between July and September 2026 across the MEDLINE/PubMed, SciELO, and Virtual Health Library (VHL) databases, as well as official portals such as ANVISA, using controlled descriptors focused on surgical site infection, surgical center, standard operating procedures, patient safety, and multidisciplinary team. The final selection comprised 10 current publications, manuals, and guidelines eligible for analysis. The review revealed that most breaks in the aseptic chain stem from unstandardized workflows and human variability in routine execution. Applying SOPs structured under Process Engineering and Lean Healthcare principles reduces cognitive failures and prevents superficial, deep, and organ/space SSIs by synchronizing the actions of surgeons, anesthesiologists, nurses, physical therapists, perfusionists, and environmental cleaning teams. Maintaining systematic audits, active epidemiological surveillance, and joint training was identified as an ongoing challenge to prevent divergence between written protocols and clinical practice. It is concluded that the integrated action of the multidisciplinary team combined with strict adherence to SOPs is indispensable for patient safety in the Surgical Center. Consolidating clear protocols, continuously monitoring aseptic indicators, and fostering a collaborative institutional culture are crucial to improving perioperative care and ensuring safe surgical procedures free from preventable harm.

title: Regulation versus Reaction Reduced to PNBA: Four Bands on the TL Ruler, and Two Gears More Than 2 TL Apart
abstract: People process at different resolutions, and this article treats processing style as a gear rather than a diagnosis. Each APPA (Adaptive Predictive Pattern Assistant) axis is scored from 10 to 50 and read on the TL ruler: one answer step is one notch of TL/10, so a score s sits at (s − 10)/10 TL. The ruler has four bands, each exactly one TL wide: L (10–19), S (20–29), F (30–39) and I (40–50). Every band edge is a whole TL, the Big Five dominant-axis cut at 40 is the I band floor at exactly 3.0 TL, and the edges 24 and 38 of the earlier three-band scale sit at 1.4 and 2.8 TL. Two behaviors that look alike from outside have opposite physics. Regulation, the I band's gear, is a steady discharge of Behavior with Pattern held, so torsion τ = B/P falls. Reaction, the L band's gear, is a spike of Behavior that starts a stalled system moving, so τ rises. An L-band score and an I-band score are always at least 21 points apart, with the whole S and F bands between them, and differ by more than 2 TL, so one axis cannot be in both gears at once. The Shatter threshold scales with Pattern, B = TL · P, so the same Behavior reads differently at different Pattern: at B = 0.08 an S-band axis with P = 0.8 is Locked while an L-band axis with P = 0.3 is in Shatter, and the I-band threshold at P = 1.2 is four times the L-band threshold at P = 0.3. title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Adolescents with Congenital Heart Disease and Obesity: A Systematic Review
abstract: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Adolescents with Congenital Heart Disease and Obesity: A Systematic Review examines what is known about using glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs)—including semaglutide, liraglutide, and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists such as tirzepatide—to treat adolescents with congenital heart disease (CHD) and overweight or obesity. Obesity is a significant and potentially modifiable health concern for young people with CHD. However, this group is physiologically diverse: cardiac anatomy, ventricular function, prior surgeries, rhythm history, oxygen levels, medications, and exercise capacity differ substantially. These factors may affect both the potential benefits of weight-loss treatment and the consequences of side effects such as nausea, vomiting, reduced fluid intake, or dehydration. Although GLP-1 RAs have shown weight-loss and metabolic benefits in adolescents without a CHD restriction, their effectiveness and cardiac safety in adolescents with CHD have not been established. The project’s primary purpose is to identify and appraise evidence relevant to adolescents aged 10–19 years with CHD and overweight or obesity. Because direct studies in this population are lacking, the review also considers two distinct sources of indirect evidence: GLP-1 RA studies in adults with CHD or heart transplants, and paediatric obesity or type 2 diabetes trials that did not report CHD-specific outcomes. Keeping these evidence streams separate helps clarify what is known directly, what is inferred, and where uncertainty remains. Following a PRISMA-guided approach, the review searched published literature and clinical-trial records through 7 November 2026. Eligible evidence included clinical trials and observational reports, with outcomes such as changes in body weight or BMI, glycaemia and other cardiometabolic measures, treatment discontinuation, adverse events, and cardiac or Fontan-specific outcomes. Study limitations and the certainty of evidence were also considered. Since no eligible comparative studies in adolescents with CHD were found, results were synthesised narratively rather than pooled statistically. The central finding is that **no identified study directly evaluated GLP-1 RA treatment outcomes in adolescents with CHD**. Paediatric trials in populations without a CHD restriction indicate that these medicines can reduce BMI or improve glycaemic control, depending on the drug and the population. Gastrointestinal effects were common, and gallbladder events occurred in some trials. Small retrospective studies in adults with CHD reported weight loss, but their designs and incomplete adverse-event reporting limit conclusions about cardiac safety. None of the paediatric trials reported outcomes for a CHD subgroup. The expected contribution of the review is a careful summary of the evidence gap and a practical account of why results from general paediatric trials cannot automatically be applied to adolescents with complex congenital physiology. Particular considerations include preload dependence and dehydration risk in Fontan circulation, potential concerns in cyanotic or systemic right-ventricle physiology, and the importance of distinguishing fat loss from loss of lean mass. These are reasons for individualised clinical consideration, not established GLP-1 RA harms specific to CHD. Overall, the review suggests that GLP-1 RAs may offer weight and metabolic benefits, but efficacy and cardiac safety in adolescents with CHD remain uncertain. Its intended outcomes are to support informed, appropriately cautious clinical discussion; identify priorities for CHD-specific monitoring; and guide future research. Recommended next steps include recording GLP-1 RA exposure and cardiac outcomes in existing registries, reporting CHD characteristics in paediatric trials, and conducting prospective studies that assess both metabolic response and outcomes relevant to cardiac physiology, growth, development, and body composition.

title: Engineering the topology of multienzyme glycoside hydrolase complexes reveals distinct effects on soluble and insoluble polysaccharide degradation
abstract: Background: Plant cell walls are structurally complex, and certain anaerobic microorganisms cope with this complexity by producing a wide range of glycoside hydrolases (GHs) organized into multienzyme complexes, the cellulosomes, to release oligosaccharides as a carbon source. Owing to their intrinsic flexibility, determining how the spatial organization within these assemblies influences catalysis remains a major challenge. Results: We used the Jo–In protein pair, which spontaneously forms a covalent isopeptide bond, to hold fused enzymes in rigid, defined arrangements. Three cellulosomal GHs from Acetivibrio thermocellus (At Cel8A, At Cel9R and At Xyn11A) were assembled into a library of 12 tri-enzymatic Jo-In complexes. Toward soluble polysaccharides, the assemblies largely preserved the activity of the free enzymes, whereas their efficiency varied markedly on insoluble substrates such as wheat bran and wheat straw. Mass spectrometry revealed that the oligosaccharide product profiles depended more on the substrate type than on the assembly architecture, although “cellulolytic” and “xylanolytic” assemblies produced distinct oligosaccharides on wheat straw. SAXS revealed similar global dimensions but different interdomain arrangements, with no significant correlation between interdomain distances and product profiles. Conclusions: Enzyme topology affects the kinetics of insoluble biomass degradation, although it has little effect on activity on soluble substrates. These effects are predicted neither by soluble-substrate activity nor by pairwise interdomain distances alone, indicating that parameters such as enzyme orientation, accessibility and conformational freedom must also be considered. The Jo-In platform provides a framework to separate these contributions in the design of programmable multienzyme complexes.

title: Lipid disorders in children
journal: Journal of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes
abstract: Childhood dyslipidemia is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and hypertriglyceridemia-associated pancreatitis. This article provides a practical algorithm-based approach to the evaluation and management of lipid disorders in children. It outlines the classification of dyslipidemias, indications for screening, diagnostic evaluation, and risk stratification. Evidence- based dietary measures, lifestyle interventions, and pharmacotherapy, including newer lipid-lowering agents, are summarized together with treatment thresholds and therapeutic targets. Diagnostic algorithms, tables, and management pathways facilitate clinical decision-making, while key referral red flags and cascade screening strategies are highlighted to promote early diagnosis and prevention of long-term cardiovascular complications.

title: Performance of a paediatric oncology trigger tool for identifying adverse events and no-harm incidents: a multicentre retrospective record review and reviewers’ perspectives
abstract: Background Despite major therapeutic progress, paediatric oncology involves complex care pathways in which safety risks extend beyond single hospital admissions and treatment-related toxicity. Patient safety measurement therefore needs methods that identify adverse events and no-harm incidents across inpatient, outpatient and home healthcare settings. Unlike many inpatient-centred paediatric trigger tools, the context-specific Paediatric Oncology Trigger Tool (POTT), developed within the Patient Safety in Paediatric Oncology study, addresses this broader context. The aim was to evaluate the performance of the POTT during retrospective record review and to describe reviewers’ perspectives on trigger relevance and usefulness. Methods This multicentre retrospective record review study, with complementary reviewer survey data, included patients aged 1–17 years who had an oncological disease and were resident in the catchment area of one of the two participating Swedish paediatric oncology centres at the time of diagnosis. Patient records from regional healthcare providers, including university hospitals, affiliated county hospitals and regionally organised home healthcare, were reviewed from diagnosis through day 90 using the POTT. Trigger yield was summarised, positive predictive values (PPVs) were calculated overall and for adverse events and no-harm incidents, and reviewer ratings and free-text comments on trigger relevance and usefulness were analysed. Results The study included 199 patients; triggers were found in 95.5% of records, with 5,883 trigger findings overall. The overall event PPV was 81.3%; adverse event and no-harm incident PPVs were 76.3% and 5.0%, respectively, with the latter rising to 10.6% when restricted to triggers applicable to no-harm incident detection. Reviewer ratings showed high relevance and more variable usefulness ratings. Free-text comments helped explain these ratings, indicating that PPV described trigger precision, whereas reviewer input reflected relevance to patient safety in paediatric oncology care and practical applicability during record review. Conclusions The POTT showed high overall performance when applied in paediatric oncology record review. Its high trigger yield and high overall event and adverse event PPVs suggest good alignment with its intended clinical context and potential to support patient safety work across the care continuum. Reviewer input added nuance beyond PPV by distinguishing trigger precision from patient safety relevance and practical usefulness.

title: O PAPEL DA LIDERANÇA NA PROMOÇÃO DA SEGURANÇA DO PACIENTE EM HOSPITAIS PÚBLICOS DE MANAUS: UMA REVISÃO INTEGRATIVA DA LITERATURA
abstract: Introdução: A segurança do paciente constitui um dos principais aspectos da qualidade da assistência hospitalar, especialmente nas instituições públicas de saúde, onde as condições organizacionais e as práticas de gestão podem influenciar na prevenção de incidentes e eventos adversos. Nesse contexto, a liderança hospitalar desempenha papel importante no fortalecimento da cultura de segurança, na comunicação entre as equipes e na construção de ambientes de trabalho não punitivos. Objetivo geral: Analisar as evidências científicas sobre a influência da liderança hospitalar na promoção da cultura de segurança do paciente, considerando sua relevância para os hospitais públicos de Manaus e da Região Norte. Metodologia: Revisão integrativa da literatura realizada nas bases PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO e LILACS (via BVS), abrangendo publicações entre janeiro de 2020 e outubro de 2026. Utilizaram-se descritores DECS/MeSH e termos livres combinados por operadores booleanos. Dos 186 registros inicialmente identificados, 153 foram excluídos na aplicação dos filtros e critérios iniciais, restando 33 estudos para a etapa de triagem de títulos e resumos; ao final, 13 artigos originais foram selecionados e analisados integralmente de forma independente por dois revisores, conforme fluxograma PRISMA 2020. Referência Bibliográfica: Plataformas digitais como as bases PubMed, SciELO e LILACS. Resultado: A síntese temática organizou-se em quatro eixos (apoio gerencial, comunicação em equipe, notificação/resposta ao erro e condições organizacionais). Os estudos demonstraram que o apoio ativo das lideranças, a liderança transformacional e autêntica e a comunicação aberta favorecem positivamente a cultura de segurança. Em contrapartida, persistem fragilidades expressivas como subnotificação de incidentes, respostas punitivas aos erros e limitações estruturais em hospitais públicos.

title: The Hospital Sector in Indonesia: Capacity, referral, emergency care, quality and cost, hospital by hospital, 2015 to 2025
abstract: How many hospitals does Indonesia have, what does each hold, where do they stand and how do patients reach them? We read the hospital sector with the hospital as the unit, counting every registered hospital, placing each in its district and asking what capacity it holds, how patients reach it, how it handles emergencies, how safe its care is and what its care costs the national health insurance (JKN). Indonesia registered 3,275 hospitals with 393,012 inpatient beds in November 2025, and 465 hospitals entered the registry between 2020 and 2025. Capacity sits in cities: 47.4% of inpatient beds stand in cities, 91.6 million residents live in districts with no class A or B hospital, and in 236 districts no hospital lists a CT service. In all, 12.3 million residents live beyond reach of a 24-hour emergency department, and 42 districts have no ventilated intensive care bed. We close with a diagnosis of where the sector falls short and with options.
