title: Analisis Kelayakan Ekonomi Penerapan Rekam Medis Elektronik Menggunakan Metode Benefit Cost Ratio
abstract: The implementation of Electronic Medical Records (EMR) requires ongoing operational costs (ongoing cost), making it necessary to evaluate the economic benefits generated. This study aimed to describe the operational costs and tangible benefits of EMR implementation and to analyze the Benefit Cost Ratio (BCR) of EMR implementation at the National Brain Center Hospital Prof. Dr. dr. Mahar Mardjono. This quantitative study was conducted at the Medical Records Unit and Hospital Information Systems Unit from December 2025 to June 2026, using document review as the data collection method. The results showed that the total operational costs (ongoing cost) for the 2020-2025 period amounted to IDR 1,415,969,150. The tangible benefits consisted of cost displacement amounting to IDR 2,547,842,757 and cost avoidance amounting to IDR 80,000,000, with a total of IDR 2,627,842,757. The BCR of 1.86 indicates that the tangible benefits were greater than the operational costs. Therefore, the BCR of 1.86 does not represent the overall economic feasibility of EMR implementation but is limited to the comparison between tangible benefits and operational costs.

title: Preventable Hospitalisation in Indonesia
abstract: How many hospital admissions in Indonesia could timely primary and community care have avoided, for whom, where and at what cost? We count the admissions that the national health insurance (JKN) pays for 124 conditions on Indonesia's list of potentially preventable hospitalisations (INA-PPH), which we built from 23 international reference lists with a panel of 22 general practitioners. In 2024 these admissions numbered 8.68 million, 53.7% of all JKN admissions, and cost Rp 41.6 trillion, 48.2% of JKN inpatient spending. Of the admissions, 32.1% followed no first-level visit in the year before, and ten conditions account for 61.0% of them. We follow each admission back through first-level visits and referral, and we set out the levers in prevention, first-level care and hospital admission that could reduce admissions.

title: Prussian blue nanozyme-based colorimetric biosensor for rapid visual quantification of β-galactosidase-positive foodborne bacteria in bottled water and milk
abstract: Infections caused by foodborne pathogens pose a serious challenge to global public health. Conventional detection approaches suffer from inherent drawbacks, e.g., time-consuming, operationally complex, high-cost, and instrument-dependent. Thus, to develop a rapid, sensitive, convenient, and cost-effective novel visual sensor for bacterial detection remains an urgent need. Herein, we rationally designed a novel sensing strategy based on β-galactosidase-positive bacteria (β-gal) can interact with a peroxidase-like nanomaterials, i.e., Prussian blue nanoparticles (PB NPs). The PB NPs-based β-galactosidase detection approach enables highly specific recognition toward β-galactosidase-positive bacteria with the linear range from 8 × 10 1 to 8 × 10 7 CFU/mL (R 2 = 0.9984). Generally, PB NPs firstly catalyze H 2 O 2 -mediated oxidation of colorless 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) and yield a blue signal (oxidized TMB, ox-TMB). Upon the trigger of target bacteria, p-aminophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (PAPG) is subsequently hydrolyzed into reductive p-aminophenol (PAP), which suppresses ox-TMB, i.e., the blue signal is negatively correlated with the bacterial concentration. The turnaround time from sample generation to measurement has been reduced by half. The novel approach achieves real-time and sensitive detection for β-galactosidase-positive bacteria flora, showing excellent feasibility, robustness, and great potential for practical applications.

title: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis: Current Therapeutic Limitations and a Critical Appraisal of Nanotechnology-based Drug Delivery Systems
abstract: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is a neglected parasitic skin infection transmitted by sand flies to humans and remains a major public health challenge in endemic regions with increasing spread into newly affected and previously non-endemic areas. The disease is characterized by disfiguring dermal lesions that can result in prolonged physical, psychological, and socioeconomic impacts. Despite its substantial global burden, therapeutic management of CL remains challenging owing to the absence of effective vaccines, inadequate efficacy and toxicity of currently used drugs, and emergence of drug-resistant Leishmania species. Conventional treatments, including pentavalent antimonials, amphotericin B (AMB), and miltefosine are associated with significant cost, safety, and compliance constraints, necessitating alternative therapeutic strategies. This critical review provides an integrated overview of epidemiology, and immunological aspects of CL while highlighting the risk factors contributing to CL spread, such as climate change and political instability. It further critically assesses current treatment strategies and their constraints, underlining the urgent need for safer and more effective alternatives. In this context, nanotechnology-based drug delivery systems have been introduced as a rational formulation approach to overcome the biopharmaceutical and pharmacokinetic challenges associated with current and emerging antileishmanial agents. Nano formulations such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles and metallic nanostructures have revealed promising preclinical results for CL. This review investigates the potential of nano-based formulations to guide and support the future development of enhanced treatment strategies for CL. Despite advancements in nanotechnology research, translational obstacles persist, including scalability, cost-efficiency and regulatory approval. Nevertheless, nanotechnology-based drug delivery systems represent a promising approach to improve the efficacy, targeting and safety profile of antileishmanial therapies, although further translational and clinical studies are required before their widespread clinical implementation.

title: Bending the Curve Early in Life: WHO Guidelines for the Integrated Management of Obesity in Children and Adolescents
abstract: The global rise of childhood and adolescent obesity requires urgent action. To address this need, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed two guidelines on people-centered, integrated management and care for (1) children and (2) adolescents with obesity, delivered through primary health care by trained multiprofessional teams. WHO strongly recommends structured dietary, physical activity, and behavior-change interventions, delivered individually or as part of multimodal interventions, for the management of obesity in children (younger than 10 years of age) and adolescents (10-19 years of age). Digital health interventions may be considered under strict parental supervision. Pharmacological interventions and bariatric surgery are not recommended for children. They may be considered for adolescents only after complete pubertal development, final adult height, and psychological stability have been achieved. Pharmacological interventions and bariatric surgery for adolescents are to be delivered in a specialized multidisciplinary setting, with close monitoring for potential adverse events over the short, medium, and long terms. The new WHO guidelines on obesity management respond to the urgent need to bend the rise of obesity in young people and complement existing public health interventions and prevention-focused guidelines. Obesity management requires action across sectors to address the social, economic, environmental, and commercial determinants of health and improve overall wellbeing. These new WHO guidelines entail coordinated multisectoral action while maintaining a people-centered approach.

title: Exploring the reasons behind delay in detection of cervical cancer in Pakistani population
journal: Journal of Pak International Medical College
abstract: Objective: To explore the factors contributing to delayed detection and treatment of cervical cancer among Pakistani women presenting with advanced disease. Methodology: This exploratory study was conducted in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Ayub Teaching Hospital, Abbottabad, Pakistan, from January to June 2025. Semi-structured, in-depth interviews were conducted with 15 patients for data collection and took about 30-45 minutes. Interviews included participants' knowledge of cervical cancer, the presentation of symptoms, health-seeking behavior, experiences of diagnosis, treatment, and family reactions, and financial constraints. We used Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis approach. Results: 15 women aged 35–55 years, with a Mean age of 46.0 ± SD years, with advanced cervical cancer were recruited. Themes that emerged from the analysis included knowledge about cervical cancer, personal behavior, sociocultural attitudes and beliefs, financial barriers, and health-system-related factors. Financial barriers included the cost of diagnostic testing, transportation, and loss of income. Health system factors covered included a lack of screening services, delayed referrals, poor patient-provider communication, poor follow-up, overcrowding of facilities, and lack of specialist services. Conclusion: Delayed cervical cancer detection resulted from interconnected patient, sociocultural, financial, and health-system barriers. Strengthening screening services, improving community awareness, ensuring timely referral, reducing financial barriers, and empowering women may facilitate earlier detection and treatment.

title: Anaesthesiologists’ integration of cardiovascular magnetic resonance findings for perioperative risk evaluation: Swiss versus international practice
abstract: Introduction Cardiovascular events account for a large share of perioperative morbidity and mortality. Because the underlying cardiac pathology varies widely between patients, cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which can detect and differentiate individual disease patterns, is a promising tool for preoperative risk assessment. Switzerland is widely regarded as a high-income country with broad access to advanced imaging technologies, including high-cost modalities such as CMR. The aim of this investigation was therefore to examine using findings from an online survey how Swiss anaesthesiologists differ in their reported use of every available CMR findings for perioperative risk evaluation compared with international respondents. Secondary aims assessed whether the integration of CMR findings in individual Swiss regions differed from that of international respondents, and whether local factors were associated with the integration of CMR findings. Methods This is a secondary analysis of an international anonymous online survey open from May 2024 to March 2025 asking if anaesthesiologists integrate findings from CMR reports into their perioperative risk evaluation when CMR reports are available. CMR integration into clinical practice was first compared between Swiss and international respondents. Regional analysis within Switzerland was then performed for six statistical regions (Lake Geneva, Swiss Plateau, Northwestern Switzerland, Central Switzerland, Zurich, and Eastern Switzerland & Ticino). Results Swiss (n = 228) anaesthesiologists more frequently incorporated CMR findings into clinical practice (77% vs. 55%, p < 0.001) compared to international colleagues (n = 148). When individual regions were assessed, respondents in Lake Geneva, the Swiss Plateau, Northwestern, and Eastern Switzerland reported higher integration of CMR findings than international anaesthesiologists, while Central Switzerland and Zurich reported equal integration. Swiss respondents were more likely to have on-site MRI than international respondents (94% vs. 82%, p < 0.001) and on-site MRI was not associated with integration of CMR findings for all Swiss (p = 0.339) or any Swiss region, but it was for international respondents (p = 0.013). Conclusions Swiss respondents integrated CMR findings into perioperative risk evaluation more frequently than international respondents. As MRI and CMR availability appear not to be limiting factors in Switzerland, further investigation is warranted to define how CMR can enhance perioperative risk evaluation.

title: Projected effects of removing pharmacists from pharmacies on access, prices and medication safety in Chile
abstract: Background Chilean law requires a pharmacist to direct every pharmacy throughout opening hours. Bill 18,719-11 would allow any pharmacy to replace the pharmacist with another health professional or a technician, arguing that cheaper direction would open pharmacies where there are none and lower prices. We assessed that argument and the safety consequences. Methods We built a societal-perspective simulation model comparing the bill with current regulation over 2027-2036. Pharmacist hours replaced determine the share of dispensings without a pharmacist, which drives additional adverse drug reactions and therapeutic-error poisonings, estimated from national hospital discharges and published data of the national poison centre. New access in municipalities without a pharmacy was valued. The increase in errors without a pharmacist and the share of harm originating in the affected pharmacies are unmeasured and were treated as scenarios. Labour-cost savings and the net health and access value were reported separately, discounted at 3%. Results In the reference scenario, 27% of dispensings would occur without a pharmacist by 2036. Over ten years the bill would add about 2,500 admissions for adverse drug reactions, 670 poisonings from therapeutic errors (28 of them admitted) and 68 deaths (95% interval 22-166). About 17,700 people would gain a pharmacy, worth CLP 12 billion (US$13 million), against CLP 150 billion (US$165 million) in health lost and care. The net health and access value was negative in 99.9% of simulations, and with any increase in errors above 3.2%. Pharmacies would save CLP 270 billion (US$296 million) in pay, lowering medicine spending by at most 0.6-1.9% if fully passed on. A favourable economic balance would require nearly three-quarters of displaced pharmacists to be re-employed immediately at the same pay. Conclusions The access and price gains are small and local, whereas the health risks would be national. They do not justify allowing every pharmacy to replace its pharmacist; access in isolated localities calls for targeted measures.

title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-in of Focal and Related Physician Experience
Bioelectric signalling: mechanisms, biological functions, diseases, diagnosis and therapy
abstract: Bioelectric signalling arises from the coordinated activity of ion channels, transporters, exchangers, and pumps, which establish the membrane potential and ionic gradients, generate endogenous electric fields, and support intercellular bioelectric coupling. These occur in both excitable and non-excitable tissues, where they interact with biochemical, mechanical, metabolic, and transcriptional networks. Excitable tissues serve as established model systems linking ion transport to rapid bioelectric activity and organ function. This review focuses primarily on the less extensively characterised roles of persistent and spatially organised bioelectric states in non-excitable and weakly excitable tissues. Evidence from the fields of development, regeneration, wound repair, immunity, and tissue remodelling suggests that bioelectric states may function as instructive signals, modulators of signalling responsiveness, permissive physiological conditions, or integrated indicators of cell and tissue state. This functional classification provides a framework for interpreting bioelectric alterations associated with cancer, fibrosis, chronic inflammation, metabolic disease, and neurological and cardiovascular disorders. We examine how membrane voltage, calcium signalling, endogenous electric fields, and gap junctional coupling interact with canonical pathways and tissue architecture. Experimental criteria are proposed to distinguish regulatory mechanisms from adaptive or secondary changes. The development of bioelectric diagnostics is evaluated in relation to analytical validity, biological interpretation, clinical validity, and clinical utility, together with therapeutic strategies based on ion channel modulation, electrical stimulation, conductive biomaterials, and bioelectronic interfaces. Integrating quantitative measurements, controlled perturbations, and computational modelling could help define when bioelectric states offer mechanistic leverage, predictive information, or clinically actionable targets.

title: Editorial: Smart sensing in plant science: advancing plant-environment interactions for sustainable phytoprotection
abstract: Plants and agricultural production play pivotal roles in maintaining ecosystem stability, ensuring global food security, and promoting sustainable agricultural development. With continued global population growth, intensifying climate change, and increasing pressure on agricultural resources, improving crop productivity, strengthening plant health monitoring and disease management, and promoting precision and sustainability in agricultural production have become major priorities in plant science and agriculture. In this context, the development of smart sensing technologies offers new opportunities to address these challenges.Smart sensing integrates sensing technologies, information processing, and artificial intelligence (AI) to enable the rapid and accurate monitoring of plant growth, health status, and environmental changes. By acquiring and analyzing multidimensional information, including plant morphology, physiological traits, disease symptoms, and environmental parameters, smart sensing facilitates crop identification, growth monitoring, plant health assessment, and agricultural product quality evaluation. These capabilities provide valuable information for plant protection, agricultural resource management, and informed decision-making in agricultural production.In recent years, advances in AI, computer vision, hyperspectral imaging, electrical sensing, and machine learning have further expanded the applications of smart sensing in plant science. In particular, the integration of deep learning algorithms with multi-source sensing technologies has provided new approaches for crop identification, plant disease diagnosis, and non-destructive assessment of agricultural products under complex agricultural conditions. This Research Topic, Intelligent visual perception plays an important role in crop identification, plant phenotyping, and precision agricultural practices. With advances in deep learning, object detection models have increasingly been applied to complex agricultural environments. However, factors such as small targets, similar background colors, overlapping leaves, and variable illumination continue to affect recognition accuracy. Collectively, these studies extend non-destructive sensing beyond external visual characteristics to the assessment of internal quality and physiological status, highlighting the value of integrating physical sensing signals with machine learning.The application of intelligent technologies also extends to agricultural decision-making, resource allocation, and sustainable production. In precision agriculture, management recommendations need to account for uncertainties in crop responses and variations in environmental conditions. Khan et al. proposed a risk-aware nitrogen recommendation framework integrating yield response modeling, conformal prediction intervals, and economic optimization. By incorporating prediction uncertainty into profit bounds, the framework determines nitrogen application rates based on conservative profit estimates and allows recommendations to be withheld when prediction uncertainty is excessively high. This approach provides a more cautious decision-making strategy for site-specific nitrogen management. Ning et al. employed life cycle assessment to investigate the combined effects of integrated organic-inorganic fertilization and cover cropping in hilly citrus orchards. Compared with other treatments, the optimized nutrient management strategy reduced carbon footprints by 26.9%-64.6% and water footprints by 75.7%-92.1%. Furthermore, compared with conventional chemical fertilization, citrus yield and economic returns increased by 33.57% and 45.51%, respectively. In addition, Abid et al. systematically reviewed 47 studies on the application of data-driven technologies in apple breeding and genetic improvement, summarizing advances in digital phenotyping, computational analysis, and genetic improvement.Their review highlighted the potential of integrating high-throughput phenotyping with data-driven approaches to accelerate breeding and improve crop traits.Collectively, these studies demonstrate the value of intelligent analysis and data-driven management in agricultural decision-making, production efficiency, and environmental sustainability.The studies in this Research Topic demonstrate the potential of intelligent sensing, multimodal detection, and data-driven approaches to advance plant science and sustainable phytoprotection. Nevertheless, challenges remain in model generalization, multi-source data integration, and the validation of model robustness under field conditions. Future research should focus on developing versatile and cost-effective sensing systems and strengthening the integration of monitoring information with agricultural decision-making. With continued advances in sensing technologies and artificial intelligence, real-time crop monitoring and precision management will become increasingly feasible, accelerating the transformation of traditional agriculture toward intelligent and information-driven production systems.

title: Rare disease diagnoses recorded in Italy: a nationwide registry-based analysis (2017–2023)
abstract: Background National rare disease registries provide essential real-world evidence for epidemiological surveillance, healthcare planning, and the assessment of territorial equity. This study aims to describe rare disease diagnoses recorded in the Italian National Rare Diseases Registry (NRDR) and examine temporal, demographic, geographical, and interregional healthcare mobility patterns. Methods We conducted a nationwide descriptive analysis of validated NRDR data recorded during 2017–2023 including sex, age at diagnosis, nosological group, region, and interregional healthcare mobility variables. Rare diseases were grouped according to the Orphanet classification and aligned with the Italian national framework. Annual reporting rates were calculated using year-specific population data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics. Cumulative national, regional, and population-weighted macroregional reporting rates used the 2023 resident population as the reference denominator. Results A total of 263,817 rare disease diagnoses were recorded. Sex was recorded as male in 42.7% of records and female in 47.4%, while sex information was missing for 9.9%. The highest annual reporting rate was observed in 2018, at 7.7 diagnoses per 10,000 inhabitants, and the lowest in 2020, at 5.0 per 10,000. Rare neurologic diseases represented the largest nosological group (17.7%), followed by rare developmental defects during embryogenesis (12.0%) and rare systemic or rheumatologic diseases (10.8%). Diagnoses were most frequently recorded among individuals aged 35–64 years, although age distributions varied substantially across nosological groups. Population-weighted cumulative reporting rates showed a clear geographical gradient, with 54.8 diagnoses per 10,000 inhabitants in Northern Italy, 51.7 per 10,000 in Central Italy, and 26.7 per 10,000 in Southern Italy and the Islands. Healthcare mobility indicators also varied considerably across regions. Conclusion The NRDR provides a broad nationwide picture of rare disease reporting in Italy and highlights substantial territorial differences in diagnostic activity and healthcare mobility indicators. Although reporting rates should not be interpreted as direct estimates of incidence, prevalence, or healthcare quality, their joint assessment with demographic and mobility indicators may support health-system monitoring and help identify areas requiring stronger diagnostic and surveillance capacity. Improved data completeness, harmonization, interoperability, and implementation of ORPHAcodes would strengthen the registry’s contribution to public health planning and European collaboration.

title: Quantum algorithms for photoreactivity in cancer-targeted photosensitizers
Development of Bootstrap-Weighted Oblique Random Forest algorithm for multiclass drug-induced liver injury prediction and risk assessment
abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) accounts for more safety-related withdrawals of approved drugs than any other adverse event. Early detection of DILI potential is a central objective of preclinical safety assessment, and computational models are now routinely applied alongside experimental assays. We propose the Bootstrap-Weighted Oblique Random Forest (BWORF), a tree ensemble that couples L 1 -sparse oblique split learning, temperature-scaled weighted bootstrap sampling, and weighted leaf-level probability estimation into a single imbalance-aware design based on Mold2 descriptors. We designed three experiments to assess BWORF’s performance by posing three critical questions: (1) does BWORF improve minority-tier detection over conventional machine learning baselines on a three-class DILI risk stratification benchmark? (2) does the BWORF design produce mechanistic behavior under controlled conditions and generalize beyond the DILI domain? (3) could improved per-compound auditability be established? For question 1, we evaluated BWORF on a DILIrank-derived benchmark harmonized from LiverTox likelihood categories into three ordered risk tiers. BWORF achieved the highest balanced accuracy and competitive macro F1 among six conventional baselines and a matched oblique-forest comparator, shifting predictive capacity toward intermediate and most-concern risk tiers at the cost of majority-tier recall and aggregate accuracy. For question 2, BWORF recovered planted causal predictors earlier than axis-aligned and unweighted oblique comparators in simulation, led the forest-variant panel on a multiclass thyroid external benchmark, and led the precision-recall ranking on a population-scale BRFSS heart-attack held-out test, with the lead emerging at full sample size. For question 3, fold-local mutual-information screening and representative LIME case studies surfaced overlapping descriptor families, supporting per-compound auditability. Altogether, the developed BWORF model could serve as a class-balancing oblique-forest extension for imbalanced biomedical tabular prediction.

title: From innovation to implementation: perspectives from Chief Health AI Officers
abstract: The emergence of the Chief Health Artificial Intelligence Officer (CHAIO) role is a defining moment in healthcare, marking the transition of artificial intelligence (AI) from an aspirational goal to a core pillar of healthcare strategy. As health systems harness AI to advance the Quintuple Aim of improving care experience, population health, cost efficiency, workforce well-being, and health equity, a growing cohort of CHAIOs is driving and accelerating AI impact 1 , 2 . To understand how CHAIO leadership is transforming health systems within the evolving AI-driven landscape, we conducted virtual semi-structured individual and group interviews with four pioneering CHAIOs from major health systems throughout the United States: Dr. Ashley Beecy of Sutter Health (San Francisco, California), Dr. Girish Nadkarni of Mount Sinai (New York, New York), Dr. Karandeep Singh of UC San Diego Health (San Diego, California), and Dr. Yasir Tarabichi of MetroHealth (Cleveland, Ohio). These leaders were selected to capture perspectives across a diverse range of operational environments. The interviews focused on four domains: the responsibilities of the CHAIO, health system transformation, current challenges, and the future trajectory of AI in healthcare. The interviews were transcribed and synthesized by identifying overarching areas of consensus—such as the need for local AI governance—while also highlighting unique insights. The insights of these four CHAIOs reveal that the mandate of the CHAIO to realize an AI-optimized health system is as much about catalyzing cross-functional collaboration and fostering cultural transformation as it is about integrating cutting-edge technology. Despite their diverse backgrounds, the interviewees consistently identified three essential competencies for the role: (1) a deep understanding of healthcare operations, (2) technical fluency in AI capabilities and their limitations, and (3) the ability to build trust across diverse stakeholder groups. Technical expertise alone was viewed as insufficient; successful CHAIOs must also be organizational strategists, skilled communicators, and change leaders.

title: Operative Note Documentation for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Against Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) Standards: A Closed-Loop Audit
abstract: Background: Operative notes are essential medico-legal documents that communicate intraoperative findings, procedural details, and postoperative management. High-quality documentation is critical for patient safety, continuity of care, and medico-legal protection and is emphasised by national standards, including Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) and the Royal College of Surgeons. Aim: To assess compliance of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative note documentation with the GIRFT Best Practice Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Guidelines (2022) and improve documentation practices through a combined quality-improvement intervention involving revision of the standardised operative note template and dissemination of initial audit findings to the surgical team. Methods: A closed-loop retrospective audit was conducted at an NHS tertiary hospital in England. Operative notes for laparoscopic cholecystectomies were assessed against 16 selected GIRFT documentation criteria. Following the initial audit cycle, the existing operative note template was revised to incorporate 14 of the 16 audit criteria, and the initial audit findings were disseminated to the surgical team through departmental presentations, emails, and an educational poster. A second audit cycle was conducted one month after implementation to assess changes in documentation quality. Compliance rates were compared between cycles using Fisher’s exact test, with p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm method. Overall documentation scores were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Results: A total of 97 laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes were reviewed in the first audit cycle and 31 in the second. Documentation improved across most criteria between cycles. The largest improvements were observed in abdominal washout volume (12.4% to 32.3%, p=0.026), local anaesthetic use and volume (75.3% to 93.5%, p=0.038), and insertion of additional ports, including location and size (87.6% to 100%, p=0.038). However, no individual criterion remained statistically significant following the Holm adjustment. The overall documentation score improved, from a median of 75.0% (IQR 68.8-81.2) to 81.2% (IQR 68.8-93.8; p=0.004). The revised template was used in only six of 31 re-audit cases (19.4%). Conclusion: Documentation quality improved following a combined quality-improvement intervention involving revision of the operative note template and dissemination of audit findings to the surgical team. Although the overall documentation score improved significantly, no individual criterion remained significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Given the low uptake of the revised template, the observed improvements cannot be attributed independently to its introduction. Further work to improve template adoption, provide targeted education, and undertake prospective reassessment is required to establish the sustainability of these improvements and further improve compliance with GIRFT recommendations.

title: Acute Cardiac Biomarker Responses to High-Intensity Interval and Continuous Running Under Matched Physiological Load in Middle-Aged Recreational Men
abstract: OBJECTIVE: High-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) is gaining popularity due to its efficiency and cardiovascular benefits. However, it remains unclear whether intermittent supramaximal exercise bouts induce greater acute cardiac biomarker responses than continuous exercise (CE) when overall physiological workload is matched. This study aimed to compare the acute cardiac biomarker responses to HIIE and CE in recreational runners under equivalent exercise conditions. METHODS: Fifteen male recreational runners (41.8 ± 8.3 years; maximal oxygen uptake [VO2max] 46.8 ± 4.1 mL·kg⁻1·min⁻1) completed 2 1-hour outdoor running sessions in a randomized crossover design with 1-2-week washout. Protocols were CE (~72% of velocity at VO2max [vVO2max]) and HIIE (12 × 1-minute intervals at ~107% vVO2max, 4-minutes recovery jogs). Blood samples were collected before (PRE), immediately after (POST), and 3 hours post-exercise (POST+3) to assess serum high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), creatine kinase-MB, and myoglobin. Heart rate, speed, and percentage vVO2max were comparable between protocols. RESULTS: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I increased significantly at POST+3 versus PRE in both protocols (P < 0.001), with no between-protocol differences. Creatine kinase-MB and myoglobin rose significantly at POST and POST+3 in both conditions (P < .05). N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide showed no significant changes between protocols. No biomarker differed between HIIE and CE at any interval, and hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP remained within clinical reference ranges throughout. CONCLUSION: When duration and workload are matched, HIIE does not elicit greater acute cardiac biomarker responses than CE, suggesting intermittent supramaximal exercise does not impose greater acute myocardial stress than CE in recreationally active middle-aged men.

title: Development of a Post-Disaster Stunting Risk Prediction System Prototype Using Agile
journal: Proceedings of The International Conference on Computer Science Engineering Social Science and Multi-Disciplinary Studies
abstract: Following a natural disaster, early detection of stunting risk among toddlers in evacuation sites is often hampered by limited time, healthcare personnel, and slow manual data recording, causing emergency nutrition intervention decisions to become less responsive to dynamic field conditions. This study aims to design and build a prototype information system for post-disaster stunting risk prediction capable of supporting fast and well-targeted nutrition intervention decisions. The system was developed using the Agile method with the Scrum framework, consisting of product backlog, sprint planning, sprint development, and sprint review and retrospective stages, allowing development to proceed iteratively and adapt to changing user needs in the field. The prototype was developed through several sprint iterations, covering shelter and toddler data management modules, anthropometric measurement input modules, and stunting risk prediction visualization modules. Testing was conducted using black box testing and a User Acceptance Test (UAT) involving prospective users, namely healthcare workers and humanitarian volunteers. The test results show that all main features functioned as intended, with a user acceptance level in the good category. The resulting prototype proved able to accelerate toddler data recording and the presentation of stunting risk information compared to the previous manual method. These findings confirm that the Agile method is relevant for developing disaster information systems that demand rapid adaptation, and the resulting prototype has the potential to serve as a foundation for developing a production system to support more responsive, data-driven emergency nutrition intervention decisions

title: An Agent-Based Modeling Framework Integrating Social Behavior into GIS Digital Twins for Smart Disaster Management
abstract: Natural hazards are not purely physical phenomena but coupled human–environment systems in which consequences are shaped by behavioral, infrastructural, and institutional dynamics interacting with physical processes. While current Geographic Information System (GIS)-based digital twins, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), have advanced our capacity to monitor and predict physical hazard dynamics, they leave the social and behavioral dimensions of disaster largely unrepresented. This gap in situational intelligence constitutes a critical failure in smart disaster management, such as evacuation gridlock, warning non-compliance, and cascading infrastructure failures triggered by human decisions. This chapter discusses Cognitive Spatial Intelligence Systems (CSIS) as a new framework that addresses this gap by integrating five intelligence layers: Spatial Intelligence (GIS), System Intelligence (digital twins), Predictive Intelligence (AI and machine learning), Social Behavioral Intelligence (agent-based modeling, ABM), and Decision Intelligence (Environmental Decision Support Tools, EDST). Each layer answers a distinct scientific question that the others cannot resolve: where, what is happening, what will happen, how will people and systems respond, and what should we do. The chapter traces the evolution of spatial intelligence from static cartography through digital twins to CSIS; argues for ABM as the behavioral simulation engine for coupled human–environment hazard systems; and grounds the framework in the California wildfire system as a case study. This framework lets emergency managers anticipate behavioral responses, including evacuation decisions, traffic bottlenecks, warning compliance, and physical hazard forecasts. Integrating social simulation into operational digital twins will shift disaster management from reactive response toward active, behavior-aware decision support.

THE SALAHI ACUTE RECOVERY CAPSULE (SARC) A Deployable Aerial Surgical and Intensive-Care System for Disaster and Conflict Zones
abstract: SARC in Brief SARC is a flying, self-contained surgical and intensive-care unit for disaster and conflict zones. A single Surgical Group is made of five spheres, each about 8 feet (2.44 metres) across, joined in a line by magnets and mechanical couplers. From one end to the other, the spheres hold fuel and a generator, fluids and a water-purification plant, the patient capsule, surgical and medical supplies, and a battery. Each sphere carries four arms with four heavy-lift turbines on each arm, so every sphere can fly on its own if the group must separate. Large cargo aircraft carry SARC units in carrier pods to the nearest working airport. Heavy helicopters carry those pods into the affected region and set them down. The units then fly up to about 100 kilometres to reach injured people, land, and unfold. The capsule sphere opens, like folding paper in reverse, into a cylinder about 6 feet across and 8 feet long, holding a rotating patient cradle and a sealed bath. The patient lies in warm fluid with the head out through a soft neck seal, supported, monitored, and connected to separate circuits for blood, brain fluid, and gut support. Robotic arms, controlled by a remote surgeon and assisted by artificial intelligence, operate on the patient while the wound stays submerged. The bath water is made on site from local water that is filtered, purified, and tested before use, which removes the need to fly hundreds of kilograms of water. Fluids that enter the body are carried sterile. A planning simulation in this document estimates that most trauma patients reach a stable state for transfer in about three to four days, and that severe brain injuries and burns may take up to about eight days. Long-term brain recovery work, described in earlier SARC drafts, continues afterwards at fixed SARC Hub hospitals. SARC is deployed to designated civilian-affected zones. Inside those zones it treats everyone in need according to medical urgency, carries no weapons, and protects its data and hardware against capture. It is designed to be tested first on computer models, synthetic tissue, lab-grown human tissue, donated bodies, and donated organs, before any use in a living patient.

Urban Climate Adaptation and Corporate Patient Capital: Evidence from China's 2017 Pilot Program
journal: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
abstract: This study estimates how China's 2017 climate-adaptive city pilot program affected corporate patient capital among nonfinancial A-share firms over 2009–2023. The baseline covers 30,748 firm-year observations in 248 cities. With firm and year fixed effects and the full set of controls, the difference-in-differences estimate is 0.1315 log points, equivalent to 10.7% of the index's sample standard deviation. The positive estimate persists under alternative measures, pre-policy matching and weighting, sample adjustments, and separate controls for concurrent city policies. The event-study estimates are positive and significant at the 10% level in event years 2–5 after implementation. Among the financing components, the first strategic equity measure shows the clearest response. The pilot estimates also indicate lower disaster losses and a smaller affected population, alongside greater supply-chain resilience. Annual reports show stronger green strategic orientation, wider environmental and sustainability disclosure, and more frequent long-term managerial language. Together, the financing and operating results identify patient capital as a corporate outcome associated with municipal climate adaptation.

title: Digital Twins and Mobile-Enabled Monitoring to Support Hospital Operational Resilience During Disruptions: A Scoping Review
abstract: Operational disruptions—including sudden demand surges, natural disasters, hospital information system (HIS) outages, and cyberattacks—threaten workflow continuity and essential healthcare delivery. Digital twins (DTs), supported by real-time operational data and mobile health (mHealth) monitoring, offer a dynamic platform for status tracking, scenario testing, and crisis decision support. This scoping review aims to map the existing evidence on how digital twins support hospital operational resilience during disruptions. The review follows the Arksey and O'Malley framework with Levac et al. enhancements and is reported according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Systematic searches are conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar up to October 2026. Original studies investigating digital twins or data-connected simulation models in hospital disruptions and operational resilience are included and classified into "direct digital twin" and "adjacent simulation" evidence. The expected outcomes include mapping the types of hospital disruptions addressed, examining coverage across resilience phases (anticipation and preparedness, response and adaptation, and post-disruption recovery and learning), and identifying key gaps in real-time integration, standardized data governance, and semantic interoperability.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Monitoring
Perceived Stress, Psychological Well-Being, and Work–Life Balance Among Health Care Workers Two Years After the 2023 Kahramanmaraş Earthquakes: A Cross-Sectional Study
journal: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness
abstract: Objective Two years after the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes, we examined perceived stress, psychological well-being, and work–life balance among health care workers and their associated factors. Methods This cross-sectional study included 413 health care workers at a tertiary hospital in Malatya, selected by stratified random sampling. Participants completed the Flourishing Scale, the Perceived Stress Scale-14, and the Work–Life Balance Scale. Groups were compared with non-parametric tests, associations were examined using Spearman correlation, and independent associations were assessed using multivariable linear regression. Results Median scores were 43 (well-being), 27 (perceived stress), and 54 (work–life balance). Perceived stress correlated inversely with well-being and work–life balance, which were positively correlated. In adjusted models, working more than 40 hours per week and living in temporary container housing were independently associated with lower well-being, lower work–life balance, and higher stress; male sex and a psychiatric history were associated with higher stress. Conclusions Two years on, modifiable occupational and post-disaster living conditions—workload and unresolved displacement—rather than earthquake exposure itself, were most strongly associated with impaired mental health and work–life balance. Regulating working hours and accelerating housing recovery may complement psychosocial support.

title: Direct Interaction Distillation: Transferring Combinatorial Knowledge Between Deep Neural Networks
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses a high-capacity Teacher Deep Neural Network (DNN) into a compact Student by transferring the knowledge encoded by the Teacher. Existing methods transfer either the Teacher DNN output distribution on images or its internal representations, yet neither utilizes how the Teacher DNN composes predictions across image regions, namely which regions are informative individually, which contribute synergistically, and which carry similar information and thus are mutually redundant. In this paper, we propose Direct Interaction Distillation (DID), a KD method that transfers this knowledge. DID partitions each image into regions, evaluates Teacher and Student on randomly masked region subsets, and matches their rewards on these inputs, i.e. their confidence in the correct class. Because masked rewards and Harsanyi interactions, which quantify the joint contribution of every subset of regions, are related by a fixed invertible transform, matching the two DNN rewards on all masked inputs is equivalent to matching their full interaction structure. DID therefore transfers this structure, using only Teacher DNN outputs, which keeps it applicable to black-box Teachers. Extensive experiments on five fine-grained benchmarks, a largerscale one, and real-world Natural Disaster Management (NDM) imagery, against a comprehensive set of logit-based and feature-based baselines and across four Student DNN architecture families in both CNN-to-Transformer and Transformer-to-CNN directions, show that DID is the strongest output-only method and improves corruption robustness, while demonstrating that the gains originate from the matched quantity, the Teacher DNN confidence in the correct class, rather than from the masked inputs alone.

title: Vulnerability Exposed: The removal of exposure from the IPCC's definition of vulnerability and its downstream implications
abstract: Across its six assessment reports, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has defined vulnerability in three ways, and exposure’s role has shifted each time. Exposure was the starting point of analysis in the Second Assessment Report, a component of vulnerability (alongside sensitivity and adaptive capacity) in the Third and Fourth, and a separate determinant of risk (that sits outside vulnerability altogether) from the Special Report on Managing the Risks of Extreme Events and Disasters (SREX, 2012) onward. Separating exposure from vulnerability obscures the fact that the two are mutually constitutive; for example, a household that cannot afford serviced land builds on the floodplain, so the flood that follows is a consequence of poverty rather than a coincidence alongside it. A vulnerability definition that keeps exposure outside cannot represent that entanglement, in which social and economic processes drive exposure and vulnerability in unison rather than as independent, coincident factors. This would matter little if exposure’s definitional change were confined to glossaries. However, measurement frameworks and funding instruments inherit their categories from upstream definitions, and measuring vulnerability is often a precondition for allocating adaptation aid and triaging populations. From AR1 to AR6, we assemble a typology of how the concept of exposure has evolved. We recompute a widely used vulnerability screening index to indicate the implications of these conceptual shifts. Across the 177 countries with complete data, removing exposure from the concept of vulnerability shifts the average country by 10.3 rank positions. Six of the forty most vulnerable states fall out of that group, and six less exposed states take their places, using identical data. A change made as definitional housekeeping reaches the allocation of adaptation finance.

title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for Flood Risk Prediction: A Comparative Study of Base Classifiers and Voting Ensembles
abstract: Floods are among the most destructive natural hazards and have considerable impacts on human life, infrastructure, agriculture and economic stability worldwide. The rise in the frequency and severity of flood events caused by climate variability and environmental changes has led to a pressing demand for precise and effective flood risk prediction systems. Traditional hydrological models are often based on complex simulations, extensive physical parameters and require a lot of computational resources, which limits their applicability for rapid decision making. Machine learning (ML) techniques offer a promising alternative by extracting complicated patterns from environmental data and producing dependable predictive outcomes. However, existing studies are mostly limited to individual algorithms or computationally intensive models, and little attention has been paid to the comprehensive comparative analysis among classical ML approaches with interpretable frameworks. In this study, we develop a machine learning-based flood risk prediction framework using the Flood Prediction Dataset from Kaggle. Nine machine learning algorithms were systematically evaluated including Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naive Bayes (NB), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, AdaBoost and LightGBM. Also, the study looked into ways of merging features to find the optimal predictive configuration. The experimental results indicate that Logistic Regression has the best individual performance with accuracy of 85.73%, precision of 86.15%, recall of 85.84% and F1-score of 85.99%. The results show that a straightforward interpretable ML model can predict flood risks successfully and with a competitive performance to complex ensemble methods. The proposed framework provides a lightweight and practical solution for supporting the early flood warning and disaster management applications.

title: How Deep Is Your Bench? Winning the Emergency Response Challenge
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In a case the author recalls from procurement practice, cranberry buyers who could not get enough berries turned to the next source down, and every buyer turned to the same one. That second source could not meet them all. Emergency plans fail the same way. A plan counts its people, vehicles, and suppliers, and it names a backup for each. The backup is often named in other plans too, or it is struck by the same event, or it is gone when the call comes. This paper takes a coach's question, how deep is your bench?, and turns it into a working test for emergency planning. The question rests on the term "co-committed resources," which names resources counted as available by more than one independently developed plan, where no shared record reveals the overlap and nothing guarantees release when several plans call at once (Treglia, 2026a, 2026c). The paper traces the question from sports to procurement, where buyers ask how fast a supplier can retool, whether the substitute meets the standard, and what is lost in the switch. Supply chain research shows that backups often fail together when one shock strikes a region. The paper then turns to the human bench. Behind every responder stands a system of relationships, including partners, children, relatives, neighbors, sitters, and care workers, and plans rarely count it. Studies in disaster sociology, the health care workforce, human services, and child care show the parts of that system. The armed forces serve as a contrast. Their structure can order and compel service and requires family care plans to match, which civilian employers, police agencies included, lack. Even so, an order can give way to a heavy enough need at home, and an injured or ill member cannot answer it. The paper argues that a short question travels because it is easy to copy, easy to recognize, and easy to understand, and it closes with ways to ask the question at each stage of planning. A deep bench is one whose players are counted once and stand clear of the shock that calls them. Winning the emergency response challenge means knowing how deep the bench really is before the event begins.

title: Prehospital pain management in mass casualty incidents: a scoping review
abstract: Background Effective pain management in mass casualty incidents (MCI) is critical due to the high prevalence of severe pain and its association with increased morbidity. For the purposes of this review, pain management refers to the systematic recognition, assessment, and treatment of pain using pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies, integrated with broader clinical care. MCI, defined as incidents where patient care needs exceed available resources, pose unique challenges for prehospital care providers. Casualties commonly sustain painful injuries — crush trauma, burns, penetrating wounds, fractures, and limb entrapment — yet analgesia is often delayed, under-dosed, or omitted. These challenges are magnified in Africa, where mass casualty events are increasing due to climate change and infrastructure failures. This scoping review aims to synthesize existing evidence on prehospital pain management strategies, identify gaps, and inform future research and policy development with the African context in mind. Methods Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was conducted across major medical databases covering studies published from 2005 to 2024. Inclusion criteria encompassed English-language studies addressing prehospital pain management in MCI, reporting on pain assessment, pharmacological/non-pharmacological interventions, or resource limitations. Excluded were hospital-based studies and non-evidence-based publications. Data were charted and synthesized into thematic categories. Results The review included 22 studies, highlighting significant gaps in standardised pain management protocols and documentation. Despite increasing mass casualty events across Africa, no studies originated from the continent, highlighting a critical research gap in resource-constrained settings. Key findings revealed underutilisation of analgesics, with only 3.2% of MCI activations receiving any analgesic administration. Ketamine and regional anaesthesia emerged as viable options, particularly in resource-limited settings. Major barriers included resource shortages, provider training gaps, and limited integration of pain management in triage systems—challenges particularly acute in African settings where baseline oligoanalgesia is endemic and healthcare systems operate with minimal surge capacity. Conclusion Prehospital pain management in MCI requires scalable, evidence-based protocols emphasising early analgesic administration, particularly ketamine and multimodal strategies. These findings have particular relevance for Africa, where health systems are strained and MCI increasingly common. Systemic barriers, including inadequate training and documentation, hinder effective implementation. Addressing these gaps through improved training, simplified protocols, and better resource planning can enhance patient outcomes and disaster response capabilities in resource-constrained settings.

title: Analisis Dampak Downtime Sistem Pembayaran Digital Terhadap Waktu Tunggu Pasien Menggunakan Pendekatan Interrupted Time Series Di Labkesda Kota Jambi.
abstract: Digital transformation improves the efficiency of healthcare services but creates vulnerability to technical disruptions (downtime) and cyberattacks. This quasi-experimental study analyzes the impact of digital payment system downtime on pre-laboratory waiting time (from administrative registration to entry into the sampling room) at the Regional Health Laboratory (Labkesda) of Jambi City. Retrospective secondary data from electronic logs covered 67 effective working days (41 digital-phase days and 26 manual-phase days) and were analyzed using interrupted time series regression. Initial autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson = 0.917) was corrected using the Cochrane-Orcutt transformation (final n = 66; Durbin-Watson = 2.022; R² = 0.992). Mean waiting time increased from 1.99 minutes in the digital phase to 6.86 minutes in the manual phase. Downtime was accompanied by a level increase of 4.875 minutes (β₂ = 4.875; p < 0.001) and a negative trend change (β₃ = −0.021; p = 0.002), indicating a flattening trend that possibly reflects staff adaptation to manual procedures. Downstream patient-safety risks warrant anticipation but were not measured in this study. Management is advised to develop a business continuity plan comprising backup payment channels and manual contingency standard operating procedures (SOPs).

title: Neurological vs. non-neurological onset in patients with Wilson disease-associated liver failure: a single-center retrospective study
abstract: Background Neurological manifestations may coexist with hepatic disease in Wilson disease, but neurological vs. non-neurological onset patterns in Wilson disease-associated liver failure are poorly characterized. We compared these onset groups, described psychiatric onset as a distinct subgroup, and explored clinical and laboratory differences according to strict neurological onset. Methods This single-center retrospective chart-based study included 162 unique patients with documented Wilson disease-associated liver failure hospitalized at a neurologically focused referral center in China during 2018–2023. The non-consecutive sample was assembled from two institutional datasets. Strict neurological onset, based on a structured historical onset code supported by initial-symptom narratives, was the primary phenotype. Strict neurological-onset and non-neurological-onset groups were compared with Mann–Whitney U and two-sided Fisher exact tests. Benjamini–Hochberg correction covered 18 exploratory laboratory comparisons, and sensitivity analyses assessed phenotype uncertainty. Results Strict neurological onset was recorded in 84/162 patients (51.9%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 44.2%−59.4%), leaving 78/162 (48.1%) in the non-neurological-onset group. Psychiatric onset was recorded in 8/162 (4.9%; 95% CI, 2.5%−9.4%), and either neurological or psychiatric onset in 92/162 (56.8%; 95% CI, 49.1%−64.2%). A narrative screen identified an explicit neurological or psychiatric symptom in 98/162 records (60.5%). Within the strict neurological-onset group, speech abnormality (64/84, 76.2%), tremor (59/84, 70.2%), limb motor abnormality (46/84, 54.8%), and drooling or swallowing difficulty (27/84, 32.1%) were most frequently recorded. The strict neurological-onset proportion ranged from 51.9% to 54.3% across sensitivity analyses. Available age, sex, chart-documented infection, and recorded vital status showed no clear between-group differences. None of 18 exploratory laboratory comparisons met the false-discovery-rate threshold of q < 0.05. Conclusion Neurological onset and related symptom domains were frequently recorded in this clinical sample. Because the cohort was non-consecutive and lacked standardized neurological, psychiatric, imaging, and laboratory timepoints, these proportions do not estimate population prevalence and the laboratory analyses do not establish correlates. Consecutive prospective studies with standardized assessments are needed.
